controls.name: RLHF/RLVR Reward-Model & Verifier Gaming Controls
controls.description_text: Prevent modern LLM post-training runs from over-optimizing against a flawed learned reward model, AI judge, or programmatic verifier. This sub-technique applies to RLHF, RLAIF, RLVR, GRPO/PPO-style post-training, and reward-model reranking where a policy can learn to satisfy the evaluator while degrading the true task objective. It owns the reward/verifier contract, held-out adversarial evaluator set, independent judge/verifier comparison, and promotion gate evidence for reward-model gaming, verifier false positives, sycophancy, verbosity bias, fabricated reasoning, unit-test gaming, or evaluator-specific shortcut learning.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns reward or verifier contracts, held-out adversarial evaluator sets, independent judge comparison, and promotion evidence for policy gaming of learned reward models, AI judges, and programmatic verifiers in RLHF, RLAIF, RLVR, and related post-training.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-012.005 detects and blocks evaluator-specific gaming under optimization; AID-H-012.001 engineers the base reward and shaping contract.
Policies can exploit evaluator flaws even when the high-level reward objective is sound.

AID-H-012.005 tests the optimized policy against independent reward and verifier evidence; AID-H-012.002 trains and calibrates the learned reward model.
Reward-model quality and policy resistance to reward-model gaming are separate claims.

AID-H-012.005 owns the reward-model and verifier-gaming gate; AID-H-012.003 owns broader episode-level behavioral promotion validation in an isolated environment.
A candidate can pass anti-gaming checks yet violate an unrelated action, resource, or safety constraint.

controls.name: Digital Content Watermarking & Signed Provenance
controls.description_text: Embed and verify policy-bound provenance signals on supported production release paths: VideoSeal/PixelSeal for image releases, the maintained Transformers SynthID Text generation/detector path for compatible autoregressive text systems, and C2PA Content Credentials for supported signed image, audio, or video containers. Each path binds exact artifacts, calibration or trust material, a complete policy-selected test population, and independently replayable evidence.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns supported production paths for digital-content watermark embedding and verification and C2PA-style signed provenance, with exact artifact binding, calibration, trust material, complete test populations, and replayable evidence.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-013.001 places or verifies provenance signals in generated content; AID-H-013.002 compares complete authorized suspect model bytes with a signed release fingerprint.
Content provenance and model-artifact ownership evidence apply to different assets.

AID-H-013.001 emits production provenance or watermark signals on supported release paths; AID-DV-004 plants deception markers, trap prompts, and leak beacons intended to trigger on misuse.
A general watermark is not a deception trap, and a trap marker is not universal content provenance.

controls.name: White-Box Artifact & Tensor-State Ownership Verification
controls.description_text: Compare complete, authorized suspect model bytes against a signature-verified release fingerprint by independently recomputing the full artifact-tree digest and canonical safetensors tensor-state digest. This control can establish an exact artifact or canonical tensor-state match; transformed or independently trained artifacts remain a no-exact-match finding rather than proof of unrelated origin.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns exact authorized suspect-byte comparison by recomputing complete artifact-tree and canonical tensor-state digests against a signature-verified release fingerprint. A no-match result does not prove unrelated lineage after transformation.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-013.002 independently compares suspect bytes with the release fingerprint; AID-H-003.006 produces and signs the model SBOM and provenance fingerprint manifest.
Fingerprint production and independent suspect comparison must remain separate.

AID-H-013.002 performs exact white-box artifact and tensor comparison when complete suspect bytes are available; AID-H-013.003 performs calibrated black-box behavioral challenges when only a compatible endpoint is accessible.
White-box exact match is stronger but less broadly applicable than statistical endpoint evidence.

controls.name: Black-Box Behavioral Ownership Fingerprinting
controls.description_text: Use a secret, signature-verified and independently calibrated structured-response challenge population to test a compatible suspect endpoint when investigators cannot inspect model bytes. The complete population produces a policy-bound statistical review trigger or no-trigger finding; neither outcome is an ownership verdict or a substitute for forensic and legal review.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns secret challenge execution, null calibration, complete population reconciliation, statistical scoring, and replayable black-box ownership review evidence for a compatible suspect endpoint. A trigger is not an ownership verdict.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-013.003 produces a bounded statistical review trigger from endpoint behavior; AID-H-013.002 proves exact artifact or canonical tensor-state match from authorized suspect bytes.
Behavioral similarity cannot be reported as byte or tensor identity.

AID-H-013.003 uses a preregistered statistical challenge population to test an ownership hypothesis; AID-DV-004 uses deception-specific markers and beacons to expose misuse or leakage.
Behavioral fingerprinting and trap activation have different null models and investigation claims.

controls.name: Ensemble Methods for Robustness
controls.description_text: Combine deliberately diverse models at inference time to reduce single-model failure and evasion risk under a declared aggregation, quorum, calibration, and abstention policy. Benefit is conditional: correlated members, shared training defects, transfer attacks, weak stacking models, or probability averaging can make an ensemble fail without an attacker defeating a literal majority. Validate correlated failure and adaptive attack performance against the deployed member set.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns empirical inference-time robustness from a declared, independently evaluated multi-model aggregation, quorum, calibration, and abstention policy. It does not change member training objectives or claim a formal robustness certificate.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-014 combines diverse model outputs at inference time; AID-H-001 changes a model's training objective and data to improve adversarial robustness.
An ensemble may contain adversarially trained members but does not replace their training control.

AID-H-014 provides empirical robustness evidence for the deployed ensemble; AID-H-015 proves a bounded formal property for an exact model, input, perturbation set, and verifier assumptions.
Observed ensemble performance is not a certificate.

controls.name: Certified Defenses
controls.description_text: Use sound certification methods to prove a specified robustness property for an exact model, input, perturbation set or norm, radius, verifier implementation, and numerical assumption. A certificate does not establish immunity to prompt injection, unrestricted semantic change, poisoning, extraction, unsupported operations, or attacks outside the declared threat model. Independently reproduce the certificate for the deployed artifact.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns independently reproducible formal certification of a specified robustness property for an exact deployed artifact, input, perturbation set or norm, radius, verifier implementation, and numerical assumptions, except for the fully enumerated GNN structural-perturbation certificate owned by AID-H-011.003. It makes no claim outside the declared threat model.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-015 proves a bounded formal property; AID-H-001 empirically changes training to improve resistance to declared adversarial threats.
Adversarial training can support certified models but is not itself a certificate.

AID-H-015 issues a formal bound under explicit assumptions; AID-H-014 aggregates multiple models and measures empirical robustness.
A diverse ensemble may still lack a sound certified radius.

AID-H-011.003 is the primary owner for exhaustive certification of a fixed GNN over an exact graph, target, candidate-edge universe, graph semantics, and structural radius; AID-H-015 owns other declared formal robustness properties and certification methods.
One GNN structural certificate must not receive a second PASS under the generic certified-defense control.

controls.name: System Prompt Structure & Instruction/Data Separation
controls.description_text: Design and maintain robust, unambiguous system prompts that clearly separate trusted instructions from untrusted content, state instruction precedence, and reduce the attack surface for prompt injection and jailbreak attempts. This technique focuses on structure (delimiters, namespaces), precedence (policy > system > developer > user), and safe inclusion of dynamic context. In current practitioner language, these patterns include spotlighting, datamarking, encoding, and other instruction/data separation techniques that mark untrusted content as data rather than authority.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns application-side system prompt structure, precedence, namespaces, serialization, delimiters, datamarking, and safe inclusion of untrusted dynamic context. It is defense-in-depth rather than an authorization or isolation boundary.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-016.001 separates instructions and data in application prompt construction; AID-H-016.002 changes model weights through hierarchy-aware training.
A delimiter template and a trained hierarchy are independent defense layers.

AID-H-016.001 reduces instruction confusion before the model responds; AID-H-018 enforces which runtime tools, parameters, values, and side effects are permitted.
A well-structured prompt cannot authorize an action or contain a compromised model.

controls.name: Model-Level Prompt Injection Alignment Training
controls.description_text: Fine-tune an instruction-following model so it learns a declared hierarchy between trusted instructions and untrusted data, using structured instruction-tuning examples and/or preference optimization over injection-resistant responses. This is a model-weight-level defense that complements AID-H-016.001; it is not equivalent to a delimiter-only prompt template.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns the signed hierarchy-aware training policy, training data, candidate artifact, and training receipt for model-weight-level prompt-injection alignment. It does not prove immunity or make the release and runtime authorization decisions.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-016.002 trains the model to preserve instruction hierarchy; AID-H-016.001 structures each prompt to separate trusted instructions from untrusted data.
Model training does not remove the need for deterministic prompt construction.

AID-H-016.002 produces the hierarchy-trained candidate and training evidence; AID-H-007.005 independently measures pre/post safety erosion and makes the promotion decision.
The training owner must not self-certify the candidate's safety regression.

AID-H-016.002 improves model-level resistance to instruction override; AID-H-018 remains the runtime authorization boundary for tools and effects.
Prompt-injection training cannot safely replace least privilege and action-time policy.

controls.name: Interruptible Agent Control Loops & Structured State Auditability
controls.description_text: Structure the agent control loop so an external orchestrator can regain control at bounded state transitions, inspect policy-relevant state and proposed tool actions, require approval, trip a circuit breaker, or terminate execution before a high-risk side effect. Audit structured state, policy reasons, approvals, tool calls, results, counters, and containment actions with stable correlation identifiers. Do not require, persist, or expose raw chain-of-thought or hidden reasoning traces.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns externally interruptible, bounded agent control-loop transitions and structured audit evidence for proposed actions, policy decisions, approvals, results, counters, breakers, and containment actions. It does not require raw chain-of-thought.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017.001 ensures the orchestrator can inspect, pause, approve, break, or terminate at bounded state transitions; AID-H-017.003 separates non-side-effecting planning from deterministic action selection and dispatch.
An interruptible loop can use many planning architectures, while plan-then-execute still needs interruption points.

AID-H-017.001 records typed state, actions, decisions, and outcomes; AID-H-037.001 controls access to confidential hidden reasoning traces and exceptional raw-reasoning storage.
Operational auditability should not depend on retaining chain-of-thought.

controls.name: Least-Privilege Tool Architecture
controls.description_text: At the agent tool registry and dispatch boundary, expose only allowlisted, strongly typed, single-purpose capabilities with bounded parameters, projections, cardinality, credentials, and side effects. Deny generic shell, arbitrary SQL, unrestricted HTTP, broad filesystem, and equivalent ambient-power tools unless a separately isolated and authorized control explicitly admits them. Verify the effective tool schema and backend permissions for every deployed agent version.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns architectural minimization of the effective agent tool surface through allowlisted, strongly typed, single-purpose capabilities with bounded parameters, projections, credentials, cardinality, destinations, and side effects.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017.002 designs the smallest safe tool primitives and removes ambient-power capabilities; AID-H-018.004 dynamically selects the allowed subset and budget for a particular authenticated request or session.
A narrow registry is the architectural ceiling, while dynamic scope is the current runtime grant.

AID-H-017.002 determines which granular tools should exist and what backend privilege they hold; AID-H-018.001 validates the parameters supplied to one exposed tool.
A perfectly validated generic shell remains overprivileged by architecture.

controls.name: Decoupled Plan-Then-Execute Architecture
controls.description_text: Architect the agent so that all high-level reasoning and task planning happen in a non-side-effecting LLM phase, separate from any code or tool execution. The LLM is restricted to outputting a structured plan (for example JSON with action names and parameters) and never calls tools directly. A deterministic Action Selector or Orchestrator then validates, transforms, and dispatches this plan against explicit safety policies and allowlists before invoking real tools. This combines planning and explanation separation from side-effectful actions, making it harder for hallucinated or injected instructions to directly reach infrastructure or sensitive APIs.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns architectural separation of non-side-effecting LLM planning from deterministic validation, transformation, action selection, and dispatch. The model proposes a typed plan but cannot directly invoke real tools.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017.003 separates planning from execution; AID-H-017.001 makes the overall loop interruptible and auditable at bounded state transitions.
Decoupling the phases does not by itself provide breaker, pause, or termination guarantees.

AID-H-017.003 routes model plans through a deterministic dispatcher; AID-H-018 authorizes the exact tool, parameter, value flow, approval, freshness, and side effect before execution.
An Action Selector is an architectural enforcement point, not a substitute for the authorization policy family.

controls.name: Transient & Isolated State Management
controls.description_text: Design an agent's application-level working state to avoid unnecessary cross-task persistence: keep task handling stateless where practical, construct request-local state from the current authenticated task, and reload signed mission objectives from a trusted source. When a deployment retains volatile context in RAM, Redis, or another shared store, consume the runtime isolation, size, TTL, reset, and serialization evidence owned by AID-I-004.001 rather than scoring those store controls here.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns application-level statelessness, task-local state construction, cross-task persistence avoidance, and trusted mission reload. It does not own runtime context-store tenant or session isolation, size limits, TTL, reset, serialization, process teardown, or memory zeroization.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017.004 owns the application architecture that avoids or minimizes retained cross-task state and reloads the trusted mission for each task; AID-I-004.001 owns steady-state runtime enforcement for any volatile context store, including tenant and session isolation, bounded size, TTL, resets, and fail-closed serialization.
A stateless design can consume AID-I-004.001 evidence when a store exists, but retained-state TTL and isolation receive only the AID-I-004.001 outcome.

AID-H-017.004 controls application-level state ownership and lifetime; AID-I-001 controls process, container, sandbox, filesystem, and runtime teardown or zeroization.
Application expiry does not prove low-level execution residue was removed.

controls.name: Agent Behavior Contract Definition & Signing
controls.description_text: Codify an agent's intended capabilities, tool and data scopes, network destinations, risk classes, approval requirements, and contract validity into a signed, machine-readable behavior contract. Bind the contract to the exact agent identity, release, policy version, issuer, and expiry, then publish it as a verified input to runtime authorization.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns definition, review, signing, publication, rotation, revocation metadata, and delivery evidence for an agent behavior contract bound to exact identity, release, capabilities, data and tool scopes, destinations, risk classes, approvals, policy, and expiry. The contract is not an allow decision.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017.005 publishes the signed agent-wide behavior contract; AID-H-018.002 evaluates the current action against active policy and verified context.
The contract supplies authority facts but never pre-authorizes every request.

AID-H-017.005 defines what the agent as a whole is intended to do; AID-H-018.007 validates and enforces the narrower permission manifest of each installed skill.
Agent-level authority and skill-level authority are nested but independently enforced.

controls.name: Agent Delegation-Graph Bounds & Capability Attenuation
controls.description_text: Constrain protocol-neutral multi-agent delegation graphs so authority can only attenuate as work is re-delegated. Bind each hop to the root principal, task, parent delegation, target agent, allowed capabilities, expiry, path, and policy-defined maximum depth; reject loops, repeated agents, scope widening, expired links, and unverifiable lineage before dispatch.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns protocol-neutral end-to-end delegation lineage, root-principal and task binding, hop and loop bounds, capability attenuation, expiry, and rejection of scope widening before dispatch.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017.006 constrains authority across a multi-agent delegation chain; AID-H-004.004 proves the discovered agent endpoint and advertised capability record.
A verified route does not authorize delegation through that agent.

AID-H-017.006 validates whole-chain delegation bounds and attenuation; AID-H-004.003 validates each receiver-side message, task transition, replay state, and communication binding.
Secure per-hop transport does not prevent scope widening across the end-to-end graph.

controls.name: Dual-LLM Isolation Pattern
controls.description_text: Implement a Privileged-LLM and Quarantined-LLM split to isolate raw untrusted data from privileged planning and tool execution. The quarantined path alone may read raw web pages, email, retrieved documents, or tool output and has no privileged tools; it emits a bounded typed result. The privileged path plans from trusted instructions and validated typed data rather than raw untrusted content.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns enforced separation of raw-content parsing from privileged planning through independent data, process, network, credential, and tool boundaries. A two-model pipeline alone is not a complete security boundary, and every proposed action still requires canonical authorization.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017.007 separates raw untrusted content into an unprivileged model path; AID-H-016.001 structurally marks and separates instructions from data inside a prompt.
Process and credential isolation provide a stronger architectural boundary than prompt formatting, but both can apply.

AID-H-017.007 limits which model path can see raw content or hold privileged tools; AID-H-018 authorizes the exact action proposed by the privileged path.
Schema-valid typed output from the quarantined model can still be malicious or misleading and must not bypass authorization.

controls.name: Tool Parameter Constraint & Schema Validation
controls.description_text: Define strict, machine-readable schemas for each agent tool's input parameters and enforce validation before execution, including types, formats, ranges, enums, cardinality, and bounded dangerous-string rules. Reject structurally invalid or prohibited parameter values before they reach authorization or execution; filesystem-object confinement for valid path values remains in AID-H-018.009.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns deterministic schema, type, format, range, enum, cardinality, and dangerous-string validation for the parameters of one tool call before execution. It does not decide whether the caller is authorized or whether a valid value may flow to the destination.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.001 determines whether parameters satisfy the tool's structural contract; AID-H-018.002 determines whether the verified subject and context are authorized to invoke the action.
Well-formed input can still be unauthorized.

AID-H-018.001 asks whether each parameter is syntactically valid; AID-H-018.005 asks whether the specific runtime value and its provenance may flow to that sink.
A valid email address or URL can still be an unauthorized exfiltration destination.

AID-H-018.001 validates calls to an exposed tool; AID-H-017.002 determines whether that tool should exist as a narrow, single-purpose capability and what backend authority it holds.
Parameter validation cannot make an ambient-power tool least privilege.

AID-H-018.001 determines whether a path value satisfies the tool's structural contract; AID-H-018.009 proves which filesystem object that value actually opens or affects.
A syntactically valid path can still escape through links, mounts, aliases, or replacement races.

controls.name: Policy-Based Access Control
controls.description_text: Externalize fail-closed authorization decisions for model- or agent-triggered tool and service operations. Derive subject, workload, tenant, delegation, and run context from trusted identity; resolve caller-visible handles through an authoritative registry; authorize the exact canonical object, type, version, action, and context; and enforce the decision at the final adapter or service boundary. Reject stale, revoked, wrong-type, cross-tenant, cross-run, or ambiguously resolved objects without revealing whether another tenant's object exists.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns fail-closed runtime allow or deny decisions for non-MCP model- or agent-triggered tool and service operations from verified subject, workload, tenant, run, delegation, tool, canonical object, type, version, action, environment, and policy attributes. It owns authoritative opaque-handle resolution and final-adapter enforcement for those paths, but not filesystem resolution, inference shared-memory topology, MCP-local object policy, or generic authorization for unrelated APIs.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.002 evaluates the current request against active policy; AID-M-009.002 defines the approved authority envelope and action-risk classification supplied to that policy.
An envelope is not a standing allow decision.

AID-H-018.002 returns the authorization outcome; AID-M-009.003 proves the acting identity, original authority, delegation lineage, credential scope, and normalized authorization context.
Identity and delegation evidence are policy inputs rather than authorization results.

AID-H-018.002 enforces policy for the exact action; AID-H-017.005 publishes the signed agent-wide behavior contract.
The contract constrains policy but cannot authorize execution by itself.

AID-H-018.002 produces the canonical runtime authorization decision; AID-D-003.003 monitors those decisions, failures, and bursts for suspicious patterns.
Enforcement and independent detection of enforcement outcomes must remain separate.

AID-H-018.002 authorizes each read or write to a canonical mutable object for the verified tenant, principal, and run; AID-H-017.004 defines the ownership, isolation, retention, provenance, and expiry architecture for transient working state.
Per-operation authorization does not make cross-run state architecture safe, and state isolation does not authorize an object operation.

AID-H-018.002 authorizes the verified subject, action, and canonical object; AID-H-018.009 proves which filesystem object an authorized path actually opens or affects.
Business authorization does not make pathname resolution race-safe.

AID-H-018.002 authorizes application and service objects used by model- or agent-triggered operations; AID-H-032.002 isolates inference queues, caches, shared memory, IPC state, warm workers, and failover placement by tenant.
A shared policy engine may support both controls, but their populations, enforcement points, evidence, and PASS results remain separate.

AID-H-018.002 owns authorization at an external non-MCP application or service boundary; AID-H-034.003 owns the MCP handler's local tool, tenant, backend, and MCP-owned object checks.
When an MCP handler calls an external service, it may consume that service's decision without awarding a second PASS for the same external-object authorization, but it still enforces its own MCP request boundary.

AID-H-018.002 authorizes an application or service object whenever a non-MCP operation presents an opaque handle; AID-H-034.006 owns MCP-specific cross-call handle issuance, binding, expiry, revocation, and per-use lifecycle.
Do not recreate MCP handle lifecycle in this protocol-neutral policy control.

controls.name: High-Impact Independent Validation & Approval Gate
controls.description_text: Before executing a high-impact tool call such as a payment, infrastructure change, code execution, or knowledge-base/memory write, require an independent validation channel and, when policy requires it, fresh step-up or human approval bound to the exact immutable action plan. The enforcement adapter verifies every signature, identity, action digest, expiry, evidence reference, and policy version locally at the executor boundary; missing or unverifiable inputs deny or degrade the action.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns independent validation and, when required, fresh step-up or human approval for a high-impact immutable action plan, including local verification of identity, action digest, signatures, evidence, expiry, policy, one-time use, and the canonical signed gate receipt.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.003 executes the runtime validation and approval gate; AID-M-006.001 defines which checkpoint exists, what evidence the operator sees, and which procedure applies.
Checkpoint design cannot issue the runtime receipt.

AID-H-018.003 issues the high-impact gate decision and receipt; AID-M-006.003 defines escalation routing, deadlines, event semantics, producer obligations, and lifecycle reconciliation.
The approval decision and the audit or escalation contract have separate owners.

AID-H-018.003 provides independent high-impact validation and approval; AID-H-018.002 provides general policy-based authorization for tool and resource access.
A policy allow may still require a separate high-impact approval receipt.

AID-H-018.003 approves the exact immutable action plan; AID-H-018.006 freshly re-verifies authorization, approval nonce, resource preconditions, and context immediately before dispatch.
Approval can become stale or misbound before use.

AID-H-018.003 enforces and records approval; AID-D-015 independently detects missing, expired, replayed, mismatched, unattended, or anomalous approval activity.
The gate cannot be the sole detector of its own bypass.

AID-H-018.003 issues the canonical approval receipt; AID-I-008.002 suspends, re-observes, binds, and resumes the exact browser action while consuming that receipt.
The browser adapter adds observation and suspension but does not create a second approval authority.

AID-H-018.003 authorizes one exact high-impact action plan after identity, policy, freshness, and approval checks; AID-H-021.005 decides whether an AI development workspace may activate its declared execution-capable surfaces.
Workspace trust is not transaction approval, and a trusted workspace cannot bypass the per-action gate.

controls.name: Intent-Based Dynamic Capability Scoping
controls.description_text:
Dynamically restrict an agent's tool capabilities per request or session based on the authenticated subject, workload, initial intent, and the exact versioned tool registry enforced by the dispatcher, instead of granting a broad static role allowlist.

How it works: The grant service intersects role, workload, and request policy, selects the smallest allowed tool set and action budget, and issues a tamper-evident signed scope whose subject, workload, registry ID/version, expiry, and budget the server verifies on every action.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns per-request or per-session capability minimization by intersecting authenticated subject, workload, intent, role, tool-registry version, expiry, and action-budget policy, then issuing and atomically enforcing a signed scope at the dispatcher. Alternate paths outside that dispatcher are not protected.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.004 chooses the smallest currently allowed subset from the tool registry; AID-H-017.002 designs the registry itself around narrow, single-purpose, least-privilege tools.
Dynamic scoping cannot make an overpowered primitive safe.

AID-H-018.004 scopes capabilities for the current request or session; AID-H-018.007 enforces the declared resource permissions of a specific installed skill.
A session grant and a skill manifest are intersecting but distinct authorization layers.

AID-H-018.004 issues the concrete runtime tool set and budget; AID-M-009.001 defines the approved degree of autonomy for Observe, Analyze, Decide, Execute, Delegate, and Persist.
Autonomy profile informs the grant but does not enumerate the exact current capabilities.

controls.name: Value-Level Capability Metadata & Data Flow Sink Enforcement
controls.description_text:
Enforce data-flow safety for agentic systems by tracking the provenance and sensitivity of runtime values (e.g., tool outputs, RAG chunks, web content) and blocking unsafe transfers into sensitive sinks (e.g., outbound email, external HTTP requests, database writes).

The gap this closes: Even if an attacker cannot change which tool is called, they may still manipulate tool parameters (e.g., recipients, URLs, file targets) to exfiltrate data. This is the critical 'data flow diversion' gap.

How it complements other controls: This sub-technique complements role-based allowlists and parameter schema validation by answering a different question: not only 'Is this parameter well-formed?' but also 'Should this value be allowed to flow to this destination?'.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns runtime provenance and sensitivity metadata for values and blocks unauthorized flows into outbound, write, model-call, retrieval, storage, and other sensitive sinks. It answers whether this value may reach this destination, not merely whether the parameter is well formed.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.005 enforces provenance-aware value-to-sink policy; AID-H-018.001 validates parameter type, shape, range, and format.
A structurally valid value can still violate data-use or exfiltration policy.

AID-H-018.005 enforces value flows at agent action and sink boundaries; AID-H-029 governs purpose, consent, retention, lifecycle stage, and authorized use of data across the broader AI lifecycle.
The sink gate consumes data-use policy but does not define the complete lifecycle authorization contract.

controls.name: Continuous Authorization Verification (Anti-TOCTOU)
controls.description_text: Prevent Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) failures in agentic workflows by re-verifying authorization at execution time for each sensitive step (not only at workflow start). Bind authorization decisions to an immutable execution context (session/task/plan + delegation chain) and invalidate stale decisions on context change.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns fresh execution-time re-verification of authorization, approval nonce, immutable action context, delegation, target resource, policy, and live preconditions before every sensitive dispatch and after pause, retry, resume, failover, or handoff.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.006 proves the approved action is still authorized and unchanged immediately before use; AID-H-018.003 performs independent validation and issues the high-impact approval receipt.
A valid receipt must still be fresh, unused, correctly bound, and consistent with live resource state.

AID-H-018.006 owns authorization freshness and anti-TOCTOU binding; AID-H-018.008 owns immutable operation identity, duplicate suppression, effect state, and uncertain-outcome reconciliation.
Fresh authorization does not prevent the same effect from being dispatched twice.

AID-H-018.006 supplies fresh execution-time authorization for the re-observed action; AID-I-008.002 owns browser request suspension and exact DOM, accessibility, method, URL, body, origin, and action re-observation.
Generic authorization freshness and browser-specific observation are composed at dispatch.

AID-H-018.006 proves authorization and live action context remain current immediately before dispatch; AID-H-018.009 binds a filesystem operation to the descriptor or handle of the object actually opened or affected.
Fresh authorization and filesystem-object confinement are composed at use but produce separate evidence and outcomes.

controls.name: Skill-Level Permission Manifest Validation & Runtime Enforcement
controls.description_text: Require every agentic AI skill to declare a structured, machine-readable permission manifest that enumerates the files, network destinations, shell capabilities, invocable tools, risk tier, and protected identity or state resources it needs. Enforce the declared boundary at install-time validation and runtime execution. The skill layer addresses scope composition in which several individually authorized tools combine into a workflow with greater authority. Protected identity and state resources use reserved logical resource IDs and require explicit elevated declarations for write access.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns the skill permission-manifest contract, schema validation, install-time permission checks, scoped credentials, and runtime interception of resource access after installation. It does not own skill content admission, enterprise inventory, agent-wide behavior contracts, or persistent-state repair.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.007 constrains one installed skill; AID-H-017.005 defines and signs the authority and intended behavior of the agent as a whole.
Skill permissions must remain within the agent contract but are independently declared and enforced.

AID-H-018.007 enforces the installed skill's declared resource ceiling; AID-H-018.004 narrows the active tool set and action budget for the current request or session.
Runtime authority is the intersection of skill permission and dynamic scope.

AID-H-018.007 controls which resource classes a skill may access; AID-H-018.005 controls whether a particular runtime value may flow to a particular sink.
Resource permission does not authorize every data flow through that resource.

AID-H-018.007 owns the permission schema and runtime enforcement after installation; AID-H-030 owns security analysis and the admission decision before a skill is allowed.
An admitted skill still requires least-privilege runtime permissions.

AID-H-018.007 denies undeclared writes to protected identity and state resources; AID-I-004.006 protects the persistence surface through baseline, diff, rollback, and file-level integrity mechanisms.
Permission enforcement and state-surface recovery are distinct layers.

AID-H-018.007 enforces permissions per installed skill; AID-M-001.003 maintains enterprise-wide skill identity, version, owner, deployment, approval, and lifecycle inventory.
Local enforcement requires but does not replace centralized visibility and revocation coordination.

AID-H-018.007 defines and intercepts the installed skill's declared file-resource ceiling; AID-H-018.009 supplies the generic descriptor- or handle-safe filesystem broker for skills and non-skill adapters.
A manifest PASS does not prove that each opened or affected object remained inside the declared root.

AID-H-018.007 enforces a skill's declared file, network, shell, tool, and protected-resource permissions after installation and activation; AID-H-021.005 decides whether the exact repository-controlled activation manifest may leave restricted mode.
Workspace trust does not grant runtime skill permissions, and a valid skill permission manifest does not authorize workspace activation.

controls.name: Tool Side-Effect Idempotency & Transaction Safety
controls.description_text: Give every state-changing tool effect a server-minted, immutable operation or business-intent ID that remains stable across authorization refreshes and policy-version changes. Execute it through an atomic action ledger, durable outbox, trusted provider registry, provider idempotency key where supported, and explicit reconciliation or compensation path. This prevents retries, duplicate queue delivery, workflow resume, approval webhook replay, and worker failover from silently repeating payments, messages, deletions, tickets, configuration changes, or other external side effects. Approval and policy versions are authorization evidence for the same operation; they must never create a new effect identity. The achievable guarantee is at-most-once effect plus reconciliation for uncertain outcomes; do not claim distributed exactly-once execution unless the effect and ledger share one transactional resource.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns immutable operation or business-intent identity, atomic action ledger, durable outbox, trusted provider binding, duplicate suppression, at-most-once effect handling, and explicit uncertain-outcome reconciliation or compensation paths for state-changing tools.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018.008 prevents repeated or inconsistent external effects; AID-H-018.006 proves the exact action is freshly authorized immediately before dispatch.
Authorization evidence may refresh without changing the stable operation identity.

AID-H-018.008 designs dispatch-time idempotency and records effect state; AID-R-007 performs post-incident authoritative readback, cancellation, reversal, compensation, and final disposition.
Recovery consumes the ledger but does not redesign the original dispatch guarantee.

AID-H-018.008 prevents duplicate external side effects; AID-H-004.003 protects peer identity, payload integrity, task state, and replay resistance in agent communication.
One message can be accepted once yet still cause duplicate provider effects after retry or worker failure.

AID-H-018.008 suppresses duplicate business effects and reconciles uncertain provider outcomes; AID-H-004.005 rejects duplicate, stale, altered, or context-misbound messages before receiver processing.
An accepted message can still produce an ambiguous external effect, so replay protection does not replace the action ledger.

controls.name: Model-Callable Filesystem Path Confinement
controls.description_text:
Control intent: Confine every model- or agent-influenced file, directory, local-resource, archive-destination, working-directory, interpreter, script, module, and executable path through a non-bypassable filesystem broker. Resolve from versioned, authenticated, operation-specific root policy and bind the decision to the filesystem object actually opened or affected. Apply separate read, create, replace, rename, delete, and execution-target permissions; fail closed on traversal, link, mount, reparse, special-file, encoding, case, replacement-race, or platform-verification ambiguity.

Applicability and outcome: This control applies when any model-callable path can reach a host or mounted filesystem. It is NOT_APPLICABLE only when no such path exists or a separately verified immutable-object or virtual-filesystem broker exposes no attacker-influenced path. PASS requires complete adapter and enabled-operation coverage for every claimed platform/filesystem profile plus independent negative-test evidence. Missing population or evidence is INSUFFICIENT_DATA; a required broker, policy, identity, OS primitive, or verifier failure is ERROR; and any unbrokered or incorrectly affected object is FAIL.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns protocol-neutral rooted filesystem resolution and confinement for model-callable read, create, replace, rename, delete, archive-destination, working-directory, interpreter, script, module, and executable paths. It binds policy and operation to the object actually opened or affected, applies platform-specific link, mount, reparse, special-file, and race controls, and proves complete adapter coverage. It does not validate parameter schemas, decide business authorization, authorize code execution, isolate processes, admit skill packages, or govern MCP publication and output semantics.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-006.002 sanitizes and releases model-generated text, markup, structured values, and URLs to a sink; AID-H-018.009 proves which filesystem object an applicable path value actually opens or affects.
A sink-safe value can still escape through filesystem resolution, and a safely opened object does not sanitize other output sinks.

AID-H-018.001 validates the path parameter's schema, type, format, and structural contract; AID-H-018.009 proves that filesystem resolution and use stay inside the authorized root and affect the verified object.
A syntactically valid path can still escape through links, mounts, aliases, or replacement races.

AID-H-018.002 decides whether the verified subject, tool, canonical resource, action, and context are authorized; AID-H-018.009 resolves the authorized filesystem scope and binds it to the object actually opened or affected.
Business authorization does not make pathname resolution race-safe.

AID-H-018.006 re-verifies authorization and live action context immediately before dispatch and after pause, retry, resume, or handoff; AID-H-018.009 owns descriptor- or handle-safe filesystem resolution and use.
Fresh authorization and opened-object confinement are composed at use but scored separately.

AID-H-018.007 defines and intercepts each skill's declared file-resource ceiling; AID-H-018.009 supplies the generic filesystem broker for skills and non-skill adapters.
A manifest PASS does not prove that every opened or affected object stayed inside its declared root.

AID-H-025.002 selects and configures the restricted interpreter and authorizes code evaluation; AID-H-018.009 confines any model-influenced interpreter, script, module, working-directory, or executable filesystem target.
Execution admission and filesystem-target confinement are separate results and neither PASS proves the other.

AID-H-030.004 safely parses and normalizes candidate skill packages before deeper admission; AID-H-018.009 confines model-callable runtime and reusable filesystem operations.
Package parsing and runtime filesystem confinement retain separate evidence and outcomes.

AID-H-034.004 governs which MCP tool, resource, prompt, schema, and UI contracts a server may publish; AID-H-018.009 confines a local filesystem object used by an applicable model-callable capability.
MCP publication approval does not prove local path confinement.

AID-H-034.005 owns MCP server output, resource-URI, template, prompt, completion, and elicitation semantics; AID-H-018.009 owns the reusable local-filesystem opened-object result for an applicable handler.
The MCP control may consume the broker receipt but must not score the same confinement result twice.

AID-I-001 contains a process, container, microVM, WASM, or other workload boundary; AID-H-018.009 confines permitted filesystem capabilities, including in-process tools that never enter a subprocess sandbox.
Isolation and opened-object confinement are independent controls and neither PASS proves the other.

controls.name: URL Normalization & Allowlist Filtering
controls.description_text: Create a safe HTTP wrapper that normalizes URLs, enforces scheme/domain allowlists, resolves DNS and blocks private/internal IP ranges, then verifies that the exact canonical URL and every redirect target are expected public resources before any background fetch, preview, or image load occurs.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns canonical URL normalization, scheme and port policy, DNS resolution, public-address validation, redirect revalidation, pinned connection, response-type and size bounds, and the decision to perform a remote fetch.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-019.001 decides whether and how a remote destination may be fetched; AID-H-002.002 validates the URL field and other request inputs supplied to inference.
Input schema validation does not prevent DNS rebinding, private-address resolution, or unsafe redirects.

AID-H-019.001 controls the network destination and bounded response bytes; AID-H-019.002 removes active HTML behavior and demotes extracted content to untrusted text.
A safely fetched page can still contain active or malicious content.

controls.name: Secure HTML Rendering & Content Demotion
controls.description_text: Strip scripts, styles, iframes, and active content; extract bounded plain text; and carry it to the model only as explicitly untrusted data. This prevents active browser content from crossing the rendering boundary and reduces the authority of indirect prompt-injection text, but does not make semantic instructions trustworthy or replace downstream tool authorization.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns safe rendering and demotion of fetched web content by removing active behavior, extracting bounded text, preserving untrusted provenance, and preventing page-controlled scripts, styles, frames, or resources from crossing into model authority.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-019.002 sanitizes content after retrieval; AID-H-019.001 authorizes the destination and performs the pinned bounded fetch.
Content demotion does not make an unsafe destination fetchable.

AID-H-019.002 strips active web behavior and labels extracted text as untrusted; AID-H-016.001 structures the final prompt so untrusted data cannot syntactically become trusted instruction.
Web sanitization and instruction-data separation are sequential defenses.

controls.name: Browser Runtime Admission & Sanitized Observation Export Gate
controls.description_text: Before browser launch, require current asset-bound receipts proving browser-context isolation, outer sandbox identity, host-profile isolation, download policy, and egress boundary. Bind receipts to the exact task and browser build, then release only bounded sanitized observations.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns admission of the browser task from current containment and egress receipts and owns the sanitized observation export gate. It does not create the browser context or enforce sandbox network egress.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-019.003 verifies context-lifecycle evidence before launch and controls observation export; AID-I-008.001 creates and destroys the ephemeral task-scoped browser context and storage partition.
The admission gate consumes rather than self-issues context-isolation receipts.

AID-H-019.003 requires and binds a current egress receipt; AID-I-001.004 enforces destination and protocol restrictions at the sandbox network boundary.
Receipt verification does not replace packet-path enforcement.

AID-H-019.003 controls whether sanitized browser observations may leave the contained runtime; AID-H-019.002 defines how HTML and active content are demoted into safe untrusted observations.
Runtime admission and content transformation are separately evidenced.

controls.name: Chunk-Level Integrity Signing
controls.description_text: Provide fine-grained RAG integrity by binding each canonical chunk, source version, embedding bytes, and embedding-model identity to a signed manifest stored in an external retention-locked trust domain, then verifying that manifest before context assembly. A hash stored beside content in the same vector database is not accepted as evidence because a vector-store writer could alter both.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns signed integrity of each canonical RAG chunk, source version, embedding bytes, and embedding-model identity using trust evidence outside the writable vector store, verified before context assembly. It proves integrity, not entitlement or truth.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-020.001 verifies fine-grained retrieval units at runtime; AID-M-002.002 verifies whole datasets, models, images, manifests, and other macro artifacts.
A valid source artifact does not prove each derived chunk and embedding remained correctly bound.

AID-H-020.001 proves the retrieved chunk and embedding are authentic and unchanged; AID-H-020.003 proves the requesting principal is entitled to read them.
Authentic content can still be unauthorized.

AID-H-020.001 protects chunks after ingestion and transformation; AID-H-002.007 verifies external source-media provenance before OCR and chunking.
Source provenance establishes the initial verdict, while chunk signing preserves integrity from that point forward.

controls.name: Source Reputation Weighting
controls.description_text: Assign and store per-chunk reputation scores based on source trust. Re-rank retrievals by combining similarity and reputation to bias toward trusted sources.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns calibrated, provenance-bound source reputation scores and their policy-approved use in retrieval ranking to prefer more trusted sources. Reputation weighting does not grant read entitlement or prove semantic truth.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-020.002 changes ranking weight from source trust; AID-H-020.003 enforces whether the current principal may retrieve each document or chunk.
High reputation never overrides access control.

AID-H-020.002 supplies source-trust ranking evidence; AID-H-020.004 enforces whether the source, release, and content are approved and fresh for current context assembly.
A reputable source can still be stale or absent from the active context policy.

controls.name: Document/Chunk-Level Permission-Aware Retrieval
controls.description_text: Enforce document- and chunk-level permissions at retrieval time so a RAG pipeline never assembles context from records the requesting principal is not entitled to read. The control mirrors source-system ACLs or relationship-based authorization metadata into chunk records during ingestion, evaluates those permissions on every query, and drops unauthorized chunks before context construction.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns query-time principal-to-document and principal-to-chunk entitlement in RAG, using source-system ACLs or relationship metadata mirrored into the index and enforced before context construction.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-020.003 proves the caller may read the chunk; AID-H-020.001 proves the chunk and embedding are authentic and unchanged.
Authorization and integrity must both pass.

AID-H-020.003 enforces caller entitlement; AID-H-020.004 enforces source approval, release binding, and freshness under the current context-governance state.
An entitled user may still be denied stale or unapproved context.

AID-H-020.003 filters documents and chunks for a principal at retrieval time; AID-I-004.002 partitions persistent memory and knowledge namespaces by tenant and trust zone.
Namespace isolation limits addressability, while entitlement applies record-level source permissions.

AID-H-020.003 answers whether the principal may read the content; AID-H-029 answers whether the data may be used for this purpose, lifecycle stage, consent state, and retention context.
Read access is not universal data-use authorization.

controls.name: Retrieval-Time Context Policy & Freshness Enforcement
controls.description_text: Enforce the signed context-source/configuration governance state produced by AID-H-021.003 on every RAG or agent-context retrieval. Before context assembly, bind each candidate chunk to the approved context release, source identifier, source-content digest, and current freshness state; reject stale, unlisted, mismatched, or unverifiable candidates.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns runtime verification and fail-closed enforcement of the signed context-source governance release, binding every candidate chunk to approved source identity, content digest, release, and current freshness before context assembly.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-020.004 enforces the current signed context-governance release on retrieval; AID-H-021.003 defines source ownership, trust tier, precedence, freshness policy, code-to-document synchronization, and release eligibility.
The retrieval gate consumes the policy rather than authoring it.

AID-H-020.004 verifies source approval and freshness; AID-H-020.001 verifies chunk and embedding byte integrity.
Fresh approved context can be tampered, and intact context can be stale.

AID-H-020.004 fails closed on unlisted, mismatched, or stale sources; AID-H-020.002 adjusts ranking according to calibrated source reputation.
Reputation is not an admission override.

AID-H-020.004 enforces context-source policy and freshness; AID-H-020.003 enforces principal-to-chunk entitlement.
Both policy dimensions must pass independently.

controls.name: Client-Side Configuration Enforcement
controls.description_text: Proactively prevents the creation and use of insecure AI agent configurations on developer endpoints. This is a 'shift-left' defense that uses endpoint security tools, policy-as-code scanners, and local development guardrails to block high-risk settings before they can ever be committed to source control or executed.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns developer-endpoint, pre-commit, repository, schema, and policy controls that prevent insecure agent configuration from being created, committed, or accepted during development.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-021.001 blocks insecure configuration before commit or build acceptance; AID-H-021.002 verifies and enforces signed configuration at agent startup and runtime.
Shift-left checks do not prove the running agent loaded the approved bytes.

AID-H-021.001 prevents unsafe workspace and agent configuration from being authored or accepted in source; AID-H-021.005 evaluates the effective workspace manifest before execution-capable surfaces activate.
A pre-commit check does not grant runtime workspace trust, and the trust gate does not replace source-policy enforcement.

controls.name: Runtime Integrity Enforcement (Signed Configurations)
controls.description_text: Ensures that an AI agent, at the moment of execution, loads and operates on runtime control artifacts that are cryptographically verified to be authentic and untampered. The primary focus is signed configuration, but the same fail-closed runtime-integrity boundary also applies to startup-loaded tool manifests and other approved integrity metadata that the service depends on before it begins work. This forms a verifiable trust chain from the secure build pipeline to the running agent.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns fail-closed verification and admission of signed startup and runtime control artifacts, configuration, tool manifests, and integrity metadata before the agent operates or reloads state. It does not semantically classify authentic content as safe.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-021.002 enforces authenticity and approved state in the running agent; AID-H-021.001 prevents insecure configuration during development.
Runtime verification remains necessary even after pre-commit policy passes.

AID-H-021.002 rejects untrusted or integrity-failed context at the runtime boundary; AID-D-004.005 verifies turn envelopes and chains and emits tamper, replay, order, or provenance findings.
The detector reports evidence, while this control owns fail-closed admission.

AID-H-021.002 proves configuration artifacts are signed and approved; AID-H-021.004 prevents the agent identity from accessing or administering the oversight surfaces that enforce those artifacts.
A valid configuration can still be dangerous if it grants self-administration of supervision.

AID-H-021.002 verifies approved startup and runtime control artifacts; AID-H-021.005 binds a workspace trust decision to the effective manifest of execution-capable surfaces.
A valid signed artifact is one input to workspace trust, not proof that every activated surface was declared and accepted.

AID-H-021.002 verifies and admits signed startup or runtime control artifacts for an agent; AID-M-001.002 inventories the release-bound model-interface tuple and reconciles effective composition across deployed replicas.
Agent configuration bytes may support both checks, but runtime admission and deployed composition reconciliation remain separate outcomes and must not be scored twice.

controls.name: Agent Context Source & Configuration Governance
controls.description_text: Govern the full set of agent-readable context sources and configuration artifacts, including runbooks, operating guides, tool specifications, escalation policies, connector definitions, and curated knowledge documents. Require explicit ownership, trust tier, freshness policy, deterministic precedence, signed critical manifests, and code-to-document change control before content is eligible for a trusted context release. Publish one current signed governance state that downstream retrieval enforcement can verify without reconstructing policy from document text.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns upstream context-source ownership, trust tier, freshness definitions, precedence, contradiction handling, code-to-document synchronization, and signed release eligibility. It does not verify runtime chunks or decide which retrieval candidates enter a live prompt.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-021.003 defines and signs the context-source governance release; AID-H-020.004 verifies and enforces that release for every retrieval candidate.
Policy authorship and runtime enforcement remain separate.

AID-H-021.003 governs operational context sources, ownership, freshness, precedence, and release state; AID-M-002 creates broader cross-lifecycle provenance, integrity, and risk-characterization records.
Context governance consumes lineage but owns the operational policy for agent-readable sources.

AID-H-021.003 decides which external context sources and configurations are eligible; AID-H-016 hardens instruction hierarchy and data separation once context is assembled.
Approved context can still be untrusted data relative to system instructions.

AID-H-021.003 governs source ownership, freshness, precedence, and release of operational context; AID-H-021.005 decides whether the workspace manifest may activate execution-capable surfaces.
Approved context governance does not establish workspace trust, and workspace trust does not approve every context source.

controls.name: Control-Plane & Oversight-Surface Isolation
controls.description_text:
Separate the agent runtime from the control plane that supervises it. A production agent must not be able to modify, disable, or bypass its own monitoring rules, policy bundles, sandbox settings, kill-switch controls, audit streams, canary definitions, oversight thresholds, egress policy, load balancers, network routes, or security groups. Keep evasion-sensitive detector internals, thresholds, canaries, and trigger logic unreadable to the runtime. An explicitly published, read-only projection of allowed tools, destinations, and public operating limits may be exposed without granting access to authoritative configuration or administration.

This control owns the single PASS for that inability; a capability-tier profile may require several independent layers, but their shared enforcement result must not be scored again.

Any break-glass path that crosses those layers requires independently authenticated quorum approval, just-in-time and time-bounded scope, tamper-evident audit, and an alert delivered through a channel the runtime cannot suppress.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns identity, network, storage, and administration separation between the agent runtime and its monitoring rules, policy bundles, sandbox settings, kill switches, audit streams, canaries, detector internals, oversight thresholds, egress policy, load balancers, routes, and security groups. It owns the one scoreable result for runtime inability to administer these surfaces, even when a capability-tier profile requires multiple independent layers.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-021.004 prevents the supervised subject from administering its own controls; AID-H-021.002 verifies that the loaded configuration artifacts are signed and approved.
Authentic configuration does not prove control-plane separation.

AID-M-009.006 defines which independent control layers a capability tier requires; AID-H-021.004 enforces and alone scores the runtime's inability to administer its oversight, egress, and infrastructure-control surfaces.
Several required layers may support one assurance conclusion, but they do not create duplicate PASS results for the same separation outcome.

controls.name: AI Coding-Agent Workspace Activation Trust Gate
controls.description_text:
Treat a newly opened, cloned, moved, aliased, or security-relevantly changed repository as an untrusted workspace before an AI coding agent activates repository-controlled behavior. Inventory lifecycle hooks, command-based MCP servers, folder-open tasks, dev-container or bootstrap commands, authority-changing agent rules, auto-approval settings, and repository-local skills or plugins without executing or authenticated-prefetching them. Keep passive bounded inspection available in restricted mode, but require an attributable user decision or exact organization policy decision bound to the canonical workspace identity and activation-manifest digest before a protected surface starts, registers, changes authority, or executes. Re-evaluate on relevant change and support immediate revocation. Workspace trust authorizes only the reviewed activation set; it never authorizes later tool actions.

Outcome states:

- NOT_APPLICABLE only when no model- or agent-influenced repository activation path exists.
- FAIL when such a path exists but the client has no non-bypassable trust boundary, or any protected activation occurs without the exact current decision.
- INSUFFICIENT_DATA when the complete activation-surface or activation-attempt population, effective binding, or required bypass-test evidence cannot be established.
- ERROR when an applicable parser, workspace-identity, policy, broker, adapter, revocation, or verifier dependency fails or becomes indeterminate.
- PASS only when every supported activation adapter is restricted before trust, every consumed decision is bound to the effective workspace and manifest, revocation and change re-evaluation work, and independent negative tests find no bypass.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns restricted-mode admission, complete repository activation-surface inventory, normalized effect preview, explicit per-workspace user decision or organization policy decision, immutable workspace and manifest binding, change-triggered re-evaluation, revocation, and proof that no protected activation occurred before a valid decision. It does not classify authentic repository content as benign, admit skill artifacts, authorize later tool effects, or provide execution isolation.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-021.001 owns development-time configuration quality and repository policy checks; AID-H-021.005 owns local restricted-before-trust activation when a workspace is opened or changes.
A pre-commit check does not prove the local client withheld repository automation.

AID-H-021.002 proves startup or runtime artifacts are signed and approved; AID-H-021.005 decides whether repository-controlled behavior may activate for this exact workspace state.
Authenticity is an input, not workspace trust or semantic safety.

AID-H-021.003 governs which context and configuration sources are eligible for a trusted release; AID-H-021.005 owns developer-client restricted mode and activation admission.
An eligible source is not automatically active in every checkout.

AID-H-030.005 admits an exact agentic skill artifact for installation or continued use; AID-H-021.005 covers the complete workspace activation surface, including non-skill hooks, tasks, servers, and settings.
An admitted skill can remain inactive until workspace trust, and workspace trust cannot admit an unreviewed skill.

AID-H-018.003 independently validates and approves an exact high-impact runtime action; AID-H-021.005 authorizes only the reviewed repository activation set.
Workspace trust must never satisfy mandatory approval for a later tool call.

AID-I-001 contains code after execution is permitted; AID-H-021.005 decides whether repository-controlled execution or registration may begin.
Restricted-before-trust admission and runtime containment are independently required where both apply.

AID-H-021.005 decides whether the exact repository-controlled activation manifest may leave restricted mode; AID-H-018.007 enforces a skill's declared file, network, shell, tool, and protected-resource permissions after installation and activation.
Workspace trust neither grants runtime skill permissions nor proves that later resource accesses stayed within the skill manifest.

controls.name: Sandboxed Dependency Installation
controls.description_text: Install dependencies only from signature-verified, promoted offline caches inside ephemeral no-network build containers with digest-pinned builders, read-only inputs, policy-derived resource limits, install-script/source-build denial, deterministic dependency-layer export, and independently signed promotion evidence. The application build consumes the exact verified layers rather than reinstalling elsewhere.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns no-network ephemeral installation of approved dependency bytes from promoted offline caches, deterministic layer export, installer execution denial, resource bounds, and evidence that the application consumed the exact produced layer.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-022.001 contains installation of immutable approved bytes; AID-H-022.002 reviews the proposed dependency change before merge.
A reviewed change still requires hostile-install containment.

AID-H-022.001 proves how approved packages were installed and which layer was consumed; AID-H-003.001 decides whether each resolved package byte is admissible.
The sandbox must consume an admission result rather than deciding package trust from successful installation.

AID-H-022.001 contains package installation; AID-H-023 verifies publisher and CI workflow provenance.
Installation isolation does not establish trusted publication origin.

controls.name: Pre-Merge Dependency Change Risk Review
controls.description_text: Block every pull request or equivalent source-change request that adds or changes a dependency until vulnerability, license, maintainer and repository reputation, release provenance, install-script behavior, and typo or homoglyph checks complete for the declared package, version, source, and lockfile diff. Unsupported or unavailable checks do not pass the change review.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns pre-merge review of a proposed dependency change for vulnerability, license, maintainer, repository, release provenance, installer behavior, name confusion, and lockfile impact. A PASS permits only the source change to proceed.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-022.002 reviews declared change intent and metadata; AID-H-003.001 independently admits the exact resolved bytes and complete dependency population later consumed.
Resolution can differ from review time, so pre-merge PASS never authorizes build or deployment.

AID-H-022.002 decides whether the proposed change may merge; AID-H-022.001 safely installs already-approved immutable bytes and proves the resulting consumed layer.
Change review and installation containment are sequential controls.

controls.name: Publisher Integrity & Workflow Hardening
controls.description_text: A critical supply chain defense that ensures software packages (e.g., NPM, PyPI) are published only from a secure, auditable, and authorized source. This technique reduces credential-only publishing attacks where a stolen developer credential is used to publish a malicious version of a legitimate package. It achieves this by prohibiting publications from local developer machines and mandating that all releases originate from a hardened CI/CD pipeline that authenticates using short-lived, identity-based tokens and generates verifiable provenance attestations.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns publisher identity, registry namespace, protected release workflow, trusted CI origin, short-lived publication authority, and provenance for released packages. It does not establish that the proposed change or exact resolved package population is safe.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-023 proves who published a package and through which authorized release workflow; AID-H-022 reviews dependency-change risk and contains installation behavior.
Trusted provenance does not make a change safe, and safe installation does not prove trusted publication origin.

AID-H-023 establishes publisher and release-path provenance; AID-H-003.001 makes the final admission decision for the exact dependency bytes and complete population consumed by build or deployment.
A valid publisher attestation is one admission signal, not authorization to consume the package.

controls.name: Fully Qualified Tool ID & Version Pinning
controls.description_text: Require fully qualified references (namespace/tool@version) for all tool calls; reject bare names and floating aliases to prevent ambiguous or hijacked resolution.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns canonical fully qualified tool identifiers and immutable version selection at resolution time. It rejects bare, floating, or ambiguous references but does not verify descriptor content or contract meaning.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-024.001 pins the tool namespace and version; AID-H-024.002 binds the descriptor bytes returned for that identity.
A fully qualified name can still serve drifted descriptor content.

controls.name: MCP Tool Descriptor Hash Binding & Drift Detection
controls.description_text: Pin MCP/tool descriptors by content hash and fail closed on drift at resolution time.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns content-hash binding and drift detection for MCP and tool descriptors at consuming-side resolution. It does not govern agent capability manifests or approve the semantics expressed by unchanged descriptor bytes.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-024.002 verifies descriptor-byte continuity; AID-H-024.001 pins the tool namespace and version used to locate those bytes.
Both bindings are required because identity and content can drift independently.

AID-H-024.002 proves that descriptor bytes match an approved digest; AID-H-024.004 decides whether the descriptor's operation, side effects, privilege, and destructive semantics are acceptable.
Byte integrity preserves meaning but does not judge it.

controls.name: Fail-Closed Ambiguous Resolution with Typosquat Detection
controls.description_text: Detect ambiguous matches and near-miss tool names and fail closed. Similarity checks must trigger explicit disambiguation rather than auto-selection.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns detection of name collisions, near misses, typosquats, and multiple eligible resolution candidates, and requires explicit disambiguation. It does not choose or authorize a candidate on similarity alone.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-024.003 blocks ambiguous or suspicious candidate selection; AID-H-024.001 requires the resulting reference to use a canonical namespace and pinned version.
Disambiguation determines the candidate, while full qualification makes that choice stable.

controls.name: Approved Tool Contract Semantics & Change Admission
controls.description_text: At onboarding and every descriptor or schema change, normalize meaning-bearing contract fields and enforce invariants over operation semantics, side effects, privilege scope, and destructive behavior. Bind the semantic-profile digest to a signed expiring approval and keep the tool unresolved when it is not approved.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns admission and change review of meaning-bearing tool-contract fields, including declared operation, side effects, privilege scope, and destructive behavior. It binds approved semantics to the exact descriptor but does not authorize a particular invocation.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-024.004 approves contract meaning; AID-H-024.002 verifies that the resolved descriptor bytes have not drifted from the approved content.
Semantic approval without byte binding is mutable, while byte binding without semantic review can preserve a dangerous contract.

AID-H-024.004 approves what a tool claims it can do before use; AID-H-034.003 validates and authorizes each request inside the MCP server handler.
An approved contract never pre-authorizes a caller, object, argument, or backend effect.

controls.name: Pre-Execution Static Analysis & Dangerous Construct Blocking
controls.description_text: Statically analyze agent- or model-generated code and other executable text immediately before merge, build, or execution, and block policy-defined dangerous constructs, malicious sinks, unsafe imports, command execution, deserialization, reverse-shell, and host-escape patterns. Bind the verdict to the exact artifact bytes, scanner/ruleset, policy version, execution request, and complete target population so code cannot change between scan and use.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns non-executing AST, SAST, and policy analysis of exact executable bytes immediately before merge, build, or execution, plus the pre-execution block decision. It cannot prove arbitrary code safe.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-025.001 blocks known dangerous constructs without running the code; AID-H-025.002 selects a restricted interpreter when dynamic evaluation is still required.
A clean static result does not remove the need for runtime language restrictions.

AID-H-025.001 is a pre-execution analysis gate; AID-I-001 owns containment of the permitted execution process, filesystem, network, and resources.
Static analysis cannot establish runtime isolation.

AID-H-025.001 provides generic dangerous-code analysis; AID-H-031.002 uses that result within provenance-aware promotion policy for AI-generated development artifacts.
The scanner verdict is one input and does not authorize merge or promotion.

controls.name: Safe Interpreter Enforcement
controls.description_text: When dynamic evaluation is required, force safe/restricted interpreters inside the execution boundary so code cannot access filesystem, network, or privileged APIs by design. For interactive 'vibe coding' run evaluation only inside ephemeral sandboxes.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns mandatory selection and configuration of a restricted interpreter when dynamic evaluation is allowed. It limits the language and API surface but is not the process, filesystem, network, or resource containment boundary.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-025.002 constrains code that is allowed to run; AID-H-025.001 decides whether exact code bytes contain policy-prohibited constructs before execution.
Interpreter restriction and static admission address different failure modes.

AID-H-025.002 restricts language semantics inside an evaluator; AID-I-001 contains the evaluator process and its operating-system effects.
A restricted interpreter escape must still meet a separate sandbox boundary.

AID-H-025.002 selects and configures the restricted interpreter and authorizes code evaluation; AID-H-018.009 confines any model-influenced interpreter, script, module, working-directory, or executable filesystem target.
Interpreter admission and opened-object confinement remain separate results, and execution permission stays with this control and AID-I-001.

controls.name: Hard-Sample Mining & Controlled Detector Retraining
controls.description_text: Systematically collect detector errors, especially false negatives on malicious prompts and false positives on benign prompts, and use them as governed hard samples for periodic retraining of the prompt injection detector. The purpose is to harden the detector against the exact decision boundaries it currently fails on. Candidate detector versions must be benchmarked against a fixed out-of-loop evaluation set and explicit promotion criteria before replacing the production detector.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns governed collection of observed false positives and false negatives, construction of hard-sample training sets, controlled detector retraining, and candidate-versus-production comparison on an independent holdout.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-026.001 learns from detector errors observed on governed samples; AID-H-026.002 deliberately generates new adversarial variants to expand coverage.
Error mining exploits known failures, while fuzzing probes for failures not yet represented.
