Runtime termination does not delete durable records that can relaunch work, while deleting a queued or scheduled record does not terminate work that is already executing.

AID-E-002 stops live execution instances; AID-E-003 quarantines or evicts malicious model, dataset, adapter, code, and configuration artifacts.
A terminated workload may be recreated from the same malicious artifact, and artifact eviction does not itself stop an already running in-memory process.

controls.name: Compromised Model Quarantine & Recovery Routing
controls.description_text: Make the exact confirmed or policy-mandated suspect model digest ineligible for serving, preserve it as incident evidence, and route the impact to detachable-adapter eviction, signed known-good rollback, clean retraining, or continued quarantine.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns quarantine and serving ineligibility of an exact suspect whole-model digest, preservation of that digest as incident evidence, and signed routing to the appropriate recovery path. Candidate backdoor scans and differential tests are inputs and do not prove quarantine or recovery completion.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-003.001 quarantines an affected whole-model digest; AID-E-003.005 detaches, tombstones, and traces compromised adapters and their derivatives.
Use adapter-level eviction when the compromised influence can be separated. Route merged or irreducible whole-model impact back to this quarantine and the applicable Restore control.

AID-E-003.001 makes a suspect model ineligible and preserves it as evidence; AID-R-001 releases a trusted rollback or newly remediated model.
Quarantine is an eviction result, not recovered-model readiness, and model recovery does not prove that the suspect digest is unavailable everywhere.

controls.name: Manifest-Bound Poisoned Dataset & Graph Eviction
controls.description_text: Remove or isolate only the exact dataset rows or graph nodes and incident edges authorized by an analyst-reviewed signed eviction manifest, and produce a new immutable artifact or governed isolation state that reflects the exact authorized set difference.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns manifest-bound eviction or isolation of exact poisoned source dataset rows, graph nodes, and incident edges, together with independent proof of the authorized set difference. Candidate detection is an input, not this control's result. It does not restore source data or operate the derived vector-index serving layer.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-003.002 removes the exact poisoned source-record or graph population; AID-R-002 restores or deterministically repairs trusted source data after eviction.
An eviction manifest proves what was removed, while recovery proves the resulting source dataset is complete and trustworthy enough for reuse.

AID-E-003.002 evicts poisoned source rows, nodes, and edges; AID-R-005 quarantines, rebuilds, validates, and cuts over the derived vector index.
Source eviction does not remove already indexed vectors or caches, and vector rollback does not prove that the malicious source records cannot be reingested.

controls.name: Confirmed Malicious Code & Persistence Eviction
controls.description_text: Evict the exact confirmed malicious deployable code and file-backed persistence artifacts enumerated in a signed incident manifest, including scripts, source or runtime configuration objects, packages, container or VM images, startup code, and file-backed persistence binaries or manifests. Preserve forensic evidence and remove or replace the affected deployable sources across the complete authoritative artifact and runtime-loaded population.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns eviction of exact confirmed malicious deployable code, scripts, packages, images, runtime configuration, startup objects, and file-backed persistence artifacts across authoritative sources and the runtime-loaded population. File-integrity monitoring, malware hunting, and candidate scanning remain detection inputs.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-003.003 removes malicious deployable code and file-backed persistence; AID-E-002 terminates active processes, jobs, pods, and workloads.
Code eviction prevents future loading but does not prove that an in-memory process stopped, while process termination leaves the deployable source intact unless this control removes it.

AID-E-003.003 removes file-backed code, configuration, and startup persistence; AID-E-005 deletes durable application schedules, queue records, webhook registrations, tool registrations, and agent state.
Application records remain owned by AID-E-005 even when malicious code originally created them.

controls.name: LLM Adapter & Derivative Artifact Removal
controls.description_text: Remove compromised LoRA, QLoRA, PEFT, prompt-tuning, or other adapter-style model artifacts from serving deployments, registries, caches, and derivative model lineage after compromise is confirmed. The objective is to stop the adapter from influencing inference or future model artifacts and to route irreducible derivatives to rollback or retraining workflows.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns incident-time detachment, quarantine, tombstone propagation, and derivative-impact tracing for compromised LoRA, QLoRA, PEFT, prompt-tuning, and other adapter artifacts across serving, registries, caches, and lineage. It routes irreducible derivative impact to rollback or retraining.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-003.005 removes a compromised adapter after an incident; AID-H-003.007 prevents unsafe adapters from loading through provenance, binding, admission, and behavioral validation.
Preventive admission does not evict an adapter already present in serving or derivatives, and incident-time removal does not replace future admission enforcement.

AID-E-003.005 detaches and tombstones compromised adapters and traces derivatives; AID-R-001.001 restores an exact known-good model or adapter attachment state.
Rollback consumes eviction evidence but does not prove that the compromised adapter or derivative is unavailable across every registry, cache, and serving route.

AID-E-003.005 removes detachable adapter influence and identifies irreducible derivatives; AID-R-001.002 builds and validates a newly remediated model when clean detachment or rollback is insufficient.
Retraining does not itself prove adapter eviction, while adapter removal does not establish the replacement model's clean utility or incident-attack resistance.

controls.name: Incident Exploit-Path Closure Verification
controls.description_text: After applicable eviction is complete and the canonical Harden or Restore owner has produced signed fix evidence, independently verify that the exact exploited path is closed across the complete incident-defined affected population. Bind the population to immutable asset, workload, service, release, fix-artifact, and policy identities; read back effective versions, configurations, policies, routes, and enforcement state using a separately credentialed verifier; then replay the exact exploit plus policy-defined negative, bypass, stale-state, and partial-rollout cases from an independent vantage point. Accept closure only when every applicable affected target consumes the exact approved fix and every required replay shows that the exploited path can no longer reach the protected effect. An omitted target, missing or unverifiable fix receipt, unavailable readback, incomplete replay population, verifier error, deployment-tool success response, or owner assertion cannot establish closure.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns independent incident-scoped verification that the exact exploited path is closed across the complete affected population after the canonical Harden or Restore owner supplies signed fix evidence. It does not implement or inherit the patch, configuration, authorization, isolation, or recovered-artifact result.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-004 verifies closure of the exact exploited path for the incident-defined population; AID-R-004 propagates the proven remediation across the wider affected fleet and future baselines.
Incident closure evidence is an input to fleet propagation, but it does not prove organization-wide rollout or recurrence prevention.

controls.name: Compromised Durable Application Session & Agent State Teardown
controls.description_text:
When compromised durable application state is identified, remove its explicitly scoped records after active runtime containment when that containment is applicable. This control remains independently applicable when no runtime execution exists.

Eviction actions

- Delete scoped application session records without claiming bearer-token, authorization-server, or gateway-session revocation
- Purge tainted durable conversational and agent memory
- Remove unauthorized webhook and tool registrations
- Cancel unauthorized queued jobs and schedule registrations

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns teardown of explicitly scoped durable application sessions, conversational or agent memory, webhook and tool registrations, nonterminal queue records, and schedule registrations after compromise. It remains applicable when no active runtime exists and never claims identity-plane revocation or active worker termination.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-005 deletes durable application and agent state; AID-E-001 revokes credentials, authentication sessions, principals, and delegated grants.
Application teardown does not prove identity-plane eviction, and revoked identity objects do not remove durable state that could reload or reschedule compromised behavior.

AID-E-005 removes durable queue, schedule, session, memory, and registration records; AID-E-002 terminates active processes, runs, execution leases, jobs, pods, and containers.
Deleting a durable job record does not terminate a worker that already acquired it, while runtime termination does not remove the record that can launch replacement work.

AID-E-005 removes compromised durable conversational and agent state; AID-R-003.002 restores an authority-selected clean snapshot into a new isolated namespace.
Teardown is an eviction result, while restoration must separately prove that it excludes tainted, cross-tenant, post-cutoff, secret-bearing, and credential-bearing state.

controls.name: Versioned Model Rollback & Restoration
controls.description_text: Restore an incident-affected model-serving release by deploying an exact known-good version from a retention-enforced immutable backup, managed-model deployment record, prompt or guardrail configuration manifest, or adapter attachment manifest authorized by an authority-signed recovery manifest, then verify the live release through an identity outside the backup-writer and deployment trust domains.

scope_boundary.responsibility: This sub-technique owns restoration of an incident-affected model-serving release by selecting and deploying an exact authority-approved pre-incident model and serving-image pair, hosted deployment record, prompt or guardrail configuration, or adapter attachment set from immutable versioned state, then reading the live identity back through an identity outside the backup-writer and deployment trust domains before cutover. It applies only when a trustworthy prior version and trusted cutoff exist. Registry labels, endpoint names, hosted model IDs, and tool success do not authorize recovery or establish live identity. It does not quarantine a suspect model, prove adapter eviction, or build a newly remediated model.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-001.001 restores an exact trusted pre-incident version; AID-R-001.002 creates a newly remediated model through clean retraining or recovery learning.
Use rollback when immutable trusted prior state exists. Use AID-R-001.002 when rollback is unavailable, incomplete, or untrustworthy; AID-R-001.001 must not silently fall back to retraining.

AID-E-003.001 quarantines the suspect model; AID-R-001.001 deploys and verifies a separate known-good version.
AID-E-003.001 makes the suspect digest ineligible for serving, preserves it as incident evidence, and routes the incident to recovery. Successful rollback does not prove that the compromised model was quarantined everywhere.

AID-E-003.005 evicts compromised adapters and derivatives; AID-R-001.001 restores and verifies known-good model or adapter state.
AID-R-001.001 consumes quarantine and tombstone evidence but owns only the rollback and live-release verification. A restored deployment does not prove incident-time adapter eviction across serving, registries, caches, and lineage.

controls.name: Model Retraining for Remediation
controls.description_text: Build sanitized recovery-training inputs, execute a fresh retraining or recovery-learning workflow, and require the exact remediated model to meet signed clean-utility and incident-attack promotion thresholds before returning to service when rollback to a trusted prior version is unsafe or unavailable.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns construction, validation, and promotion of a newly remediated model through clean retraining or recovery learning when trustworthy rollback is unavailable, incomplete, or unsafe. It does not silently substitute rollback and does not prove that the original compromised artifact or derivative was evicted.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-001.002 creates a newly remediated model; AID-R-001.001 restores an exact trusted pre-incident version.
Use retraining when rollback state is unavailable or untrustworthy. Use AID-R-001.001 when an authority-approved immutable prior version and trusted cutoff exist.

AID-R-001.002 builds and validates the replacement model; AID-E-003.005 quarantines compromised adapters and their derivatives.
For adapter-derived compromise, this control consumes signed quarantine, tombstone, and derivative-routing evidence. Retraining does not establish that the original adapter or derivative can no longer be served.

AID-R-001.002 consumes the signed federated-client and update exclusion population when constructing sanitized recovery-training inputs and validating the remediated model; AID-I-006 owns the underlying quarantine decision and exclusion enforcement.
Retraining must not recreate or independently score client quarantine, and quarantine alone does not prove that the replacement model is safe to promote.

controls.name: Data Integrity Recovery for AI Systems
controls.description_text: Restore the integrity of source datasets used by or generated by AI systems that were corrupted, tampered with, or maliciously altered during a security incident. This includes training data, validation data, feature-store sources, source corpora that feed RAG systems, configuration data, or logs of AI outputs. Recovery typically involves reverting to known-good backups, using data validation tools to identify and correct inconsistencies, or, in some cases, reconstructing data if backups are insufficient or also compromised.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns restoration or deterministic repair of trusted source records and datasets after incident corruption, including source corpora that feed retrieval pipelines. It identifies downstream impact but does not roll back, quarantine, rebuild, or cut over a vector index namespace.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-002 restores the source records that feed retrieval; AID-R-005 restores the derived vector-index serving artifact.
Source-data recovery does not remove tainted vectors, publish anti-reingestion tombstones, rebuild a clean index, or verify the live vector alias cutover.

controls.name: Post-Incident Identity & Session Re-establishment
controls.description_text: Create new trusted interactive sessions only after incident-scoped credential and session eviction, fresh policy-required reauthentication, and a new identity-provider readback.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns creation and independent verification of new trusted interactive sessions after required eviction and reauthentication. It does not revoke prior credentials, tokens, grants, or sessions and does not restore conversational state or privileges.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-003.001 creates a new trusted interactive session; AID-E-001 evicts the compromised credential, token, session, principal, or grant population.
This recovery control consumes verified AID-E-001 results and cannot treat successful new authentication as proof that old authentication and authorization objects were revoked.

controls.name: Trusted Conversational & Agent-State Re-establishment
controls.description_text: Restore approved non-secret conversational or agent state into a new isolated namespace from the exact authority-selected pre-incident snapshot, excluding tainted, cross-tenant, post-cutoff, and credential-bearing state.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns restoration of an authority-selected clean conversational or agent-state snapshot into a new isolated namespace. It excludes tainted, cross-tenant, post-cutoff, secret-bearing, and credential-bearing state and does not perform incident-time teardown of the compromised durable state.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-003.002 restores selected clean conversational or agent state; AID-E-005 deletes compromised durable application and agent state.
The recovery snapshot must not reintroduce records removed by AID-E-005, and successful restoration does not prove that tainted state was torn down everywhere.

controls.name: Progressive Capability & Privilege Re-enablement
controls.description_text: Restore incident-affected tools, roles, permissions, delegated authority, and action edges one policy-defined tier at a time after locally verifying every prerequisite and reading back effective runtime authority.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns policy-staged re-enablement and readback of incident-affected tools, roles, permissions, delegated authority, and action edges after recovery prerequisites pass. It does not revoke the prior authority or replace per-action runtime authorization.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-003.003 progressively grants new post-incident capability state; AID-E-001 revokes the compromised credential, principal, session, and grant populations.
Re-enablement must follow verified eviction and cannot use a new privilege assignment as evidence that prior authority was removed.

AID-R-003.003 restores which capabilities are available after an incident; AID-H-018 authorizes and constrains each runtime tool action and side effect.
A restored capability tier does not itself authorize a specific invocation, parameter set, or external effect.

controls.name: Fleet Remediation Propagation & Technical Recurrence Prevention
controls.description_text: Propagate an incident-proven technical remediation across the complete affected fleet, read the resulting effective state back from every target through a separate read-only path, and institutionalize the fix in build, deployment, or configuration baselines so the same technical weakness does not recur.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns fleet-wide propagation and institutionalization of an already proven technical remediation. It excludes post-incident review facilitation, customer communication, ticket administration, and enterprise risk-scoring updates.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-004 propagates an incident-proven fix across the affected fleet and future baselines; AID-R-006 orchestrates dependency-ordered recovery of one multi-component system.
A clean-room cutover can complete without proving organization-wide propagation, while fleet remediation does not replace dependency-aware assembly and cutover of the recovered system.

controls.name: Rapid Vector Index Rollback & Quarantine
controls.description_text:
Provide fast, controlled recovery for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines after index poisoning or malicious content injection is detected. The vector index is treated as an immutable, versioned artifact.

Three-Stage Recovery

1. Rollback — Atomically roll back to a last known-good snapshot
2. Quarantine — Quarantine and preserve suspicious chunks for forensics while removing them from production retrieval
3. Rebuild — Rebuild and re-promote a clean index that enforces provenance, policy, and security approvals

Goal: Restore trustworthy retrieval quality quickly while preventing re-serving tainted data.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns vector namespace rollback, delete-by-ID quarantine, anti-reingestion tombstones, clean index rebuild, candidate validation, and alias cutover evidence after retrieval poisoning or malicious content injection. It does not restore authoritative source records, evict those source records, or provide ongoing production retrieval monitoring.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-005 restores the derived vector index and serving alias; AID-R-002 restores the authoritative source records and corpora.
This control consumes restored source data and lineage findings but separately proves that tainted vectors are excluded and the rebuilt index is live.

AID-R-005 rebuilds and promotes a clean retrieval index; AID-E-003.002 identifies and evicts the exact poisoned source-record or graph population.
A vector rollback or rebuild does not prove that malicious source records can no longer be ingested again, so this control consumes the signed eviction manifest and tombstone population.

AID-R-005 performs incident-time vector-index recovery; AID-D-014 continuously monitors production RAG content, relevance, and retrieval provenance.
Detector findings can trigger recovery, but index rollback and rebuild do not replace ongoing monitoring or finding generation.

controls.name: Clean-Room AI System Redeployment Orchestration
controls.description_text:
Orchestrate clean-room recovery of a multi-component AI system by validating an authority-signed recovery dependency manifest, executing digest-pinned workflow templates in dependency order, and reading live component state and external readiness through separate read-only paths before cutover. The manifest binds the exact component population, immutable recovery artifact for each component, trusted workflow-template digest, prerequisite control-result digest, dependency DAG, and cutover prerequisites.

Use when: recovery contains multiple components or prerequisite results whose ordering matters.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns verification of referenced prerequisite-result signatures and digests, dependency ordering, trusted recovery-workflow execution, assembled live-state readback, and cutover authorization for a multi-component recovery. Each component control retains ownership of its bounded technical result. This orchestrator does not reinterpret or replace another control's result. Missing components, unknown dependencies, cycles, mutable artifacts or workflows, unverifiable prerequisites, incomplete live populations, failed external probes, or unmet signed RTO/RPO objectives block cutover.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-006 assembles and cuts over one dependency-ordered recovered system; AID-R-004 propagates an incident-proven remediation across the affected fleet and future baselines.
R-006 may invoke component and remediation workflows, but it does not prove that every affected deployment or future build inherited the fix.

controls.name: External Side-Effect Reconciliation & Compensation
controls.description_text:
After containment, reconcile the complete incident-scoped population of externally issued agent actions against authoritative downstream state, then idempotently cancel, reverse, compensate, or explicitly disposition each unintended, duplicate, or uncertain effect under a signed incident policy. This applies to payments, messages, IAM changes, tickets, deployments, and external data mutations.

Irreversible effects: a delivered message, disclosure, physical action, or other irreversible effect cannot be erased. Compensation or signed acceptance records its final disposition; it does not claim restoration of the prior reality.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns incident-time reconciliation of externally issued agent actions against authoritative downstream state and the idempotent cancellation, reversal, compensation, or signed final disposition of each unintended, duplicate, or uncertain effect. It cannot erase an irreversible message, disclosure, or physical action; compensation or signed acceptance records the final disposition without claiming restoration of the prior reality.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-007 reconciles and remediates external effects after an incident; AID-H-018.008 designs stable action identity, idempotency, transaction safety, and compensability before execution.
R-007 consumes the action ledger or outbox and provider identifiers produced by AID-H-018.008, but preventive transaction design does not prove that an already-issued effect was reversed.

AID-R-007 remediates effects already issued to downstream systems; AID-E-005 removes compromised internal durable sessions, memory, registrations, queues, and schedules.
Deleting an internal job or session does not cancel a payment, message, IAM change, deployment, or other external effect that was already accepted downstream.

AID-R-007 proves the final disposition of each incident-scoped external effect; AID-R-006 orchestrates dependency-ordered recovery and cutover of a multi-component AI system.
R-006 may schedule R-007 as a prerequisite, but successful system cutover does not itself prove cancellation, reversal, or compensation of prior downstream actions.

AID-R-007 resolves existing incident-scoped external effects; AID-R-004 propagates the technical fix that prevents recurrence.
Institutionalizing the fix does not reverse actions already issued, while compensating those actions does not prove the weakness was removed from the fleet.

families.name: AI Asset Inventory & Mapping
families.description_text: Maintain an authoritative, versioned map of the AI estate: owned models, datasets, infrastructure, dependencies, agent skills, externally consumed AI services, and public or private AI endpoints. Reconcile declared inventory with independently observed deployment, network, identity, registry, and control-plane evidence so unknown, orphaned, stale, or unexpectedly exposed assets remain visible.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns authoritative discovery, inventory, dependency mapping, ownership, and declared-versus-observed reconciliation for the AI estate. It produces stable asset facts and drift findings but does not authorize, block, remediate, contain, or evict an asset.

families.name: Data, Artifact & Knowledge Provenance, Integrity & Risk Characterization
families.description_text: Establish version-bound provenance, integrity, and risk-characterization records for data, AI artifacts, memory, and knowledge assets.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns version-bound provenance, integrity, and content-risk reference records for data, AI artifacts, memory, and knowledge assets. It creates facts consumed by admission and runtime controls but does not admit a supplier, authorize a read or write, detect production drift, or decide release promotion.

families.name: Model Behavior Baseline & Documentation
families.description_text: Create signed, version-bound reference artifacts that describe an AI system and quantify its expected behavior. The family covers model cards and datasheets, operational and output metrics, explanation stability, agent missions, media reconstruction error, graph-model behavior, and LLM prompt-suite results.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns signed, version-bound reference artifacts that document an AI system and quantify expected behavior under governed conditions. It creates and recalibrates trusted baselines but does not claim the system is attack-free or perform live detection and alerting.

families.name: AI Secure Configuration Baselines & Release Gates
families.description_text: Define, version, review, and validate secure configuration baselines for AI infrastructure, containers, development environments, MLOps pipelines, agent runtimes, and AI service settings. Convert approved templates and applicable vendor or industry requirements into signed policy-as-code, measurable posture criteria, and build or release gates.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns design-time secure configuration baseline authoring and build or validation-time conformance criteria for AI infrastructure, containers, development environments, pipelines, runtimes, and services. Runtime posture observation belongs to Detect, while deployment and runtime enforcement belong to Harden.

families.name: Human-in-the-Loop Control Design & Readiness
families.description_text: Design and validate the human-control system for AI actions that require review, override, escalation, or emergency intervention. Define each checkpoint and timeout path, qualify the assigned operators on the exact interface and procedure, exercise the complete branch population, and maintain a canonical audit-event contract that lets an independent verifier reconcile activation through final action.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns Human-in-the-Loop checkpoint design, operator qualification and readiness, escalation topology, and audit-event contracts. It prepares and verifies the human-control system but does not make runtime authorization decisions or execute incident containment.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-M-006 designs and tests the human-control architecture and evidence contract; AID-H-018 enforces runtime tool authorization, approval, and execution-time verification.
Readiness evidence does not unlock an action, and a runtime gate does not replace checkpoint design or operator qualification.

families.name: AI Use Case & Safety Boundary Modeling
families.description_text: Define a signed, machine-readable safety boundary for an AI use case, determine which technically testable safety and conformance dimensions apply to its real architecture and impact paths, and evaluate the exact release candidate before promotion.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns intended-use and forbidden-action safety-boundary modeling, applicability classification, deterministic release conformance, and conditional statistical fairness evaluation. Adaptive adversarial security benchmarking and model-card publication remain separate controls.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-M-007 defines acceptable use, forbidden outcomes, applicable safety dimensions, and release criteria; AID-M-004 identifies adversarial threats and prioritizes technical security risk across the architecture.
A safety policy states what must hold, while a threat model explains how assets and trust boundaries may be attacked or fail.

AID-M-007 owns the signed safety boundary and its deterministic or fairness-specific release checks; AID-M-008 owns repeatable adversarial agent security benchmarking.
Passing declared conformance cases does not establish adaptive bypass resistance, and an adversarial benchmark does not define the authoritative use-case boundary.

families.name: Agent Autonomy & Authority Governance
families.description_text:
Define and version the control-plane facts that determine an agent's approved mission, functional autonomy, authority envelope, accountable runtime identity and delegation lineage, live trust state, and required control profile. The child controls partition those dimensions into separate control objectives, while preserving one chain from approved purpose to constrained runtime authority and recoverable change history.

Example: a support agent may read a knowledge base and draft replies autonomously, require approval before sending email, and be forbidden from issuing refunds or changing credentials. Its exact workload identity, delegated scope, goal-manifest digest, authority-envelope version, and current trust state must remain bound to that decision.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns signed governance facts for an agent's functional autonomy, authority envelope, runtime identity and delegation lineage, goal changes, trust state, and required capability-tier control profile. It publishes facts for enforcement but never grants an action solely from a governance artifact.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-M-009 defines and publishes the approved autonomy, authority, identity, delegation, trust-state, and control-profile facts; AID-H-018 verifies those facts at the runtime action boundary and returns the authorization outcome.
Governance states what authority should exist, while runtime enforcement decides whether the exact current action may proceed.

families.name: AI Asset Retirement, Transfer & End-of-Life Governance
families.description_text: Define formal end-of-life procedures for AI models, configurations, datasets, and related storage artifacts. This family covers retirement-time sanitization, transfer-time chain-of-custody, dual-custody elimination, and confirmation that retired or transferred assets are no longer reachable or recoverable.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns asset-lifecycle retirement, ownership-transfer closure, sanitization, de-publication, and proof that retired or transferred AI assets are no longer reachable or recoverable. It is lifecycle governance rather than generic incident-response maturity.

families.name: AI-Contextualized Data Sanitization & Input Validation
families.description_text:
Implement rigorous validation, sanitization, and filtering mechanisms for all data fed into AI systems.

Training & Fine-Tuning Data: This applies to training data, fine-tuning data, and live operational inputs (including user prompts for LLMs). The goal is to detect and remove or neutralize malicious content, anomalous data, out-of-distribution samples, or inputs structured to exploit vulnerabilities like prompt injection or data poisoning before they can adversely affect the model or downstream systems.

LLM-Specific Controls: For LLMs, this involves specific techniques like stripping or encoding control tokens and filtering for known injection patterns or harmful content.

Multimodal Systems: For multimodal systems, this includes validating and sanitizing inputs across all modalities (e.g., text, image, audio, video) and ensuring that inputs in one modality cannot be readily used to trigger vulnerabilities, bypass controls, or inject malicious content into another modality processing pathway.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns preventive validation, sanitization, normalization, quarantine, and admission controls for data and inputs before they affect training, inference, multimodal processing, or downstream AI workflows. Each child is separated by lifecycle stage, data representation, and observation point.

families.name: Secure ML Supply Chain Management
families.description_text: Apply software supply-chain security throughout the AI/ML lifecycle: admit trusted inputs, promote and distribute exact signed releases, control protected model delivery to clients or edge devices outside the enterprise trust boundary, and remediate vulnerabilities in deployed AI software. The aim is to prevent malicious, tampered, vulnerable, or unauthorized model and software bytes from entering, leaving, or remaining exploitable in the system.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns preventive admission, promotion, and distribution controls for third-party software, datasets, hardware, infrastructure definitions, models, adapters, manifests, signatures, unsafe serialized artifacts, and protected client/edge model releases outside the enterprise trust boundary, plus continuous vulnerability remediation for deployed AI application and platform software. Accelerator firmware and driver remediation remains under AID-H-009.002.

families.name: Identity, Access & Trusted Communication for AI Systems
families.description_text: Establish trusted human and machine identities, authenticate and authorize access to AI resources, verify agent discovery information, and protect security-relevant messages across communication trust boundaries. This family covers users, workloads, services, APIs, agents, data stores, tools, and administrative interfaces; its sub-techniques define the independently implementable controls.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns preventive identity, authentication, discovery provenance, communication integrity, and access controls for human users, workloads, services, APIs, agents, data stores, tools, and administrative AI surfaces.

families.name: AI Privacy & Privacy-Preserving ML (PPML) Controls
families.description_text: Apply privacy controls across AI training, fine-tuning, inference, retrieval, and embedding storage so sensitive records and derived representations are not exposed through membership inference, model inversion, memorization, vector reconstruction, or sensitive attribute leakage. This family includes cryptographic, statistical, data-centric, and storage-layer controls; it keeps the familiar PPML label while covering the broader privacy engineering surface that modern AI systems actually operate.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns privacy engineering across training, fine-tuning, inference, retrieval, embeddings, and vector storage through statistical, cryptographic, data-centric, and storage-layer controls against memorization, inversion, membership inference, reconstruction, and sensitive-data exposure.

families.name: AI Output Hardening & Sanitization
families.description_text: Apply preventive release controls to model-generated output before it reaches a user, renderer, tool, interpreter, storage sink, or downstream service. Structured text and markup require schema, sink-encoding, redaction, and streaming holdback controls; generated media and binary artifacts require independent decode, type, bounds, re-encode, malware, or quarantine gates.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns preventive release controls for generated text, markup, structured payloads, URLs, predictions, media, and binary artifacts before they reach users, renderers, tools, interpreters, storage sinks, or downstream services.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-006 sanitizes, transforms, blocks, or releases output at the preventive boundary; AID-D-003 observes output and emits policy-violation findings.
Detection evidence informs the release gate but does not itself control delivery.

AID-H-006 owns output release safety for text, markup, predictions, media, and binary artifacts; AID-H-025 owns admission and execution constraints for generated code or commands.
Rendering or releasing a code artifact and authorizing it to execute are separate decisions.

families.name: Secure Training & Evaluation Pipeline Integrity
families.description_text: Protect the integrity and reproducibility of AI training and evaluation pipelines, including governed inputs, isolated execution environments, code and dependency provenance, evaluation-corpus controls, evaluator mechanisms, raw evidence, and promotion gates. The children separate data and feedback integrity, resource and environment isolation, reproducible builds, evaluation-case and promotion-evidence integrity, trusted toolchains, secure checkpoint or intermediate artifacts, and evaluator-mechanism independence because each has a distinct measured population and enforcement point.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns integrity, isolation, reproducibility, evidence independence, evaluation sufficiency, evaluator integrity, and promotion controls across AI training, fine-tuning, post-training transformation, and validation pipelines.

families.name: Federated Learning Participant & Aggregation Security
families.description_text: Secure both participant admission and update aggregation in federated-learning architectures. The children independently control confidential aggregation, resistance to malicious or unreliable client updates, and identity/attestation/round admission for participating workloads. Enrollment establishes who may join a round; aggregation controls what accepted participants can learn or influence.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns participant admission, contribution confidentiality, and malicious-update influence control for federated-learning rounds. Enrollment decides who may submit; aggregation controls what accepted participants can reveal or influence.

families.name: AI Accelerator & Hardware Integrity
families.description_text: Implement measures to protect the physical integrity and operational security of specialized AI hardware (GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs) and the platforms hosting them against physical tampering, side-channel attacks (power, timing, EM), fault injection, and hardware Trojans. It also includes leakage across co-located tenants or jobs on shared accelerators (e.g. shared GPUs in inference clusters). This aims to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of AI computations and model parameters processed by the hardware.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns physical and operational integrity, trusted boot, custody, firmware lifecycle, device reuse isolation, and confidential execution for AI accelerators and hosting hardware.

families.name: Graph Neural Network (GNN) Poisoning Defense
families.description_text: Implement defenses to secure Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) against data poisoning attacks that manipulate the graph structure (nodes, edges) or node features. The goal is to ensure the integrity of the graph data and the robustness of the GNN's predictions against malicious alterations.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns preventive graph-data sanitization, provenance weighting, robust GNN training and architecture, and bounded structural robustness certification against graph poisoning and structural perturbation.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-011 sanitizes graph data, hardens the GNN, and issues bounded certificates; AID-D-012 emits trigger-response, structure-feature, and topology anomaly findings.
Preventive mutation and training controls remain separate from Detect-side investigation signals.

families.name: Reinforcement Learning (RL) Reward Hacking Prevention
families.description_text: Design and implement safeguards to prevent Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents and LLM post-training pipelines from discovering and exploiting flaws in reward functions, learned reward models, AI judges, or programmatic verifiers to achieve high rewards for unintended or harmful behaviors ('reward hacking'). This includes classical environment rewards, RLHF/RLAIF reward models, RLVR verifiers, reward-channel integrity, and independent evidence that policies remain aligned with intended outcomes rather than numeric reward maximization alone.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns preventive reward design, learned reward calibration, isolated behavioral promotion validation, reward-channel integrity, and judge or verifier gaming controls for RL, RLHF, RLAIF, RLVR, and related post-training systems.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-012 designs and gates reward systems to prevent exploitable optimization; AID-D-013 detects reward hacking, reward tampering, verifier gaming, and policy manipulation from observed evidence.
Preventive reward controls and production or training detection remain distinct.

families.name: Proactive Content & Model Watermarking & Fingerprinting
families.description_text: Embed governed provenance, watermark, or ownership signals into generated content and model assets so authorized investigators can trace origin, detect bounded reuse, or test a model-ownership hypothesis. Content-level controls cover supported image, video, text-generation, and signed-provenance paths; model-level controls use canonical artifact fingerprints or preregistered behavioral challenge populations.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns bounded technical provenance and ownership signals through content watermarking, signed provenance, exact white-box artifact or tensor comparison, and calibrated black-box behavioral challenges. It does not prevent copying, guarantee confidentiality, prove factual truth, or establish legal ownership.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-013 embeds or evaluates bounded provenance and ownership signals after model artifacts or generated content may be copied; AID-H-003.011 decides whether an entitled, freshly attested client may receive the decryption key for an exact protected model release.
Attribution evidence is not an entitlement decision, and attested delivery does not provide later ownership proof.

families.name: Instruction Hierarchy & Prompt Injection Hardening
families.description_text: Harden instruction-following systems at two independently deployable layers: application-side prompt structure that separates trusted instructions from untrusted data, and model-weight-level alignment training that teaches the model to preserve that hierarchy under injection attempts.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns instruction-precedence and instruction-versus-data hardening in prompt construction and model training. Neither child grants tool authority or guarantees prompt-injection immunity; runtime action authorization remains in AID-H-018.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-016 reduces the chance that untrusted content overrides instruction hierarchy; AID-H-018 independently authorizes and constrains tool actions and side effects.
Instruction robustness is defense-in-depth and cannot grant runtime authority.

families.name: Secure Agent Architecture
families.description_text: This technique covers the secure-by-design architectural principles for building autonomous AI agents. It focuses on proactively designing the agent's core components-such as its structured control loop, tool-use mechanism, state management, and action dispatchers-to be inherently more robust, auditable, and resistant to manipulation. This is distinct from monitoring agent behavior; it is about building the agent securely from the ground up.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns secure-by-design agent architecture for interruptible control loops, least-privilege tool surfaces, decoupled planning and execution, task-scoped state, signed behavior contracts, delegation bounds, and raw-content isolation. Auditability means structured state and outcomes, not raw hidden reasoning.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-017 designs the agent architecture and its control points; AID-H-018 independently enforces authorization and capability limits at each runtime action boundary.
A secure architecture must still route every effect through canonical authorization.

AID-H-017 owns structured control-loop and state auditability without requiring chain-of-thought; AID-H-037 owns reasoning-trace confidentiality, reasoning compute bounds, and provider reasoning-block integrity.
Agent audit records and hidden reasoning state have different disclosure and integrity requirements.

families.name: Tool Authorization & Capability Scoping
families.description_text:
Establish and enforce strict authorization and capability limits for tools invocable by an AI agent. Apply least privilege with allowlists, parameter boundaries, authoritative object authorization, filesystem-object confinement, mandatory structured inputs/outputs, and transaction-safe side-effect execution so authorized retries, resumptions, and duplicate deliveries cannot silently repeat high-impact actions.

This is the runtime enforcement layer for agent risk models such as the lethal trifecta (private data, untrusted content, and an exfiltration or side-effect channel in one session) and Meta's Agents Rule of Two, which limits how many of those high-risk properties may coexist without stronger gates.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns runtime enforcement of tool and action authority through parameter constraints, policy decisions, high-impact approval, dynamic capability scope, value-flow controls, filesystem-object confinement, execution-time freshness, skill permissions, and transaction-safe side effects. It independently verifies governance and HITL inputs.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-018 verifies current governance facts and enforces the exact runtime action; AID-M-009 defines and publishes autonomy, authority, identity, delegation, goal, trust-state, and control-profile facts.
Governance is policy input, while this family owns the allow, deny, degrade, or dispatch boundary.

AID-H-018 invokes and enforces human checkpoints at runtime; AID-M-006 defines checkpoint requirements, operator readiness, escalation topology, and audit-event contracts.
A ready human-control system does not itself authorize an action.

families.name: Safe Fetch & Web Content Admission for Agents
families.description_text: Prevent SSRF and malicious-web-content propagation by authorizing destinations, demoting active content, requiring task-bound browser-containment and egress receipts, and exporting only sanitized observations.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns destination admission, safe fetch, content demotion, browser-runtime admission, and sanitized observation release. It consumes but does not implement browser-context isolation or the outer sandbox network boundary.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-019 admits destinations, fetched content, browser runtime evidence, and sanitized observations; AID-I-008.001 creates, partitions, and destroys the ephemeral browser context.
Safe content admission does not prove browser state isolation.

AID-H-019 applies application-level URL and browser admission policy; AID-I-001.004 enforces the outer sandbox network egress boundary.
A URL allow decision must still be constrained by independently enforced network policy.

families.name: RAG Index Hygiene & Signing
families.description_text: Implement integrity, source-trust, context-policy, freshness, and retrieval-time authorization controls across RAG indexing and context assembly. Cryptographically bind chunks and embeddings, weight content by source trust, enforce document/chunk entitlements, and verify the approved context governance release before retrieved content reaches the model.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns preventive RAG retrieval integrity, source trust, principal entitlement, context-source policy, freshness, and fail-closed context assembly before retrieved content reaches the model.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-020 signs, authorizes, filters, and enforces RAG context assembly; AID-D-014 emits content, relevance, provenance, diversity, and coverage findings at the post-retrieval observation point.
Detect reports retrieval risk, while Harden controls which chunks may enter context.

families.name: AI Agent Configuration Integrity & Hardening
families.description_text:
This technique establishes and enforces the integrity and security of an AI agent's instructional configurations (e.g., system prompts, operational parameters, external configuration files like CLAUDE.md).

Defense-in-Depth Strategy: It combines client-side controls to prevent the creation of insecure configurations in development environments, cryptographic verification at runtime to ensure the agent only operates based on a trusted, untampered directive, context-corpus governance over external runbooks, tool specifications, and operational knowledge, restricted-before-trust workspace activation, and isolation of the runtime from its oversight plane.

Structured Format Mandate: Use structured, non-executable formats (e.g., schema-validated JSON or YAML) where the consuming platform supports them, and prevent configuration parsing from becoming an execution path. Repository-controlled activation surfaces still require an exact workspace trust decision even when their bytes are authentic and schema-valid.

This directly counters attacks where adversaries manipulate an agent's behavior or developer-machine authority through external, modified, or silently activated configuration.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns shift-left agent configuration controls, runtime signature enforcement, governed external context sources, restricted-before-trust workspace activation, and separation of the supervised runtime from its oversight and control plane.

families.name: Dependency Change Vetting & Sandboxed Installation
families.description_text: This family secures two connected but distinct stages: risk review of a proposed dependency change before merge, and isolated deterministic installation of already-approved immutable package bytes. The children provide the implementation controls for those stages.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns pre-merge dependency-change risk review and isolated deterministic installation of already-approved immutable package bytes. It does not make the authoritative final admission decision for the exact dependency population consumed by build or deployment.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-022 reviews proposed changes and contains installation; AID-H-003.001 admits the complete exact package population resolved for the build or deployment.
Review and sandbox evidence support but cannot replace final byte-level admission.

AID-H-022 owns change risk and hostile installation behavior; AID-H-023 owns publisher identity, registry workflow, trusted CI release origin, and package provenance.
A trusted publisher can ship a risky change, and a safe-looking change can come from a compromised publisher path.

families.name: Tool & MCP Resolution Integrity
families.description_text: Enforce deterministic, verified resolution of tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoints to prevent typosquatting, alias collision, and registry-based misdirection. Resolution must be fail-closed: ambiguous matches require explicit disambiguation rather than best-guess selection. This ensures that when an agent calls a tool, it binds to the exact, authorized namespace, version, and descriptor bytes intended.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns consuming-side resolution of the exact approved tool or MCP identity, namespace, version, descriptor bytes, and contract semantics, including fail-closed handling of ambiguity and drift.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-024 resolves which logical tool or MCP endpoint is intended; AID-H-028.001 authenticates the selected server transport before connection.
Correct logical resolution does not prove transport identity, and a valid connection does not prove that the intended tool contract was selected.

AID-H-024 verifies server-published descriptors from the consumer side; AID-H-034.004 governs what an MCP server is allowed to publish.
Publication approval and consuming-side resolution are independent enforcement points.

AID-H-024 decides which approved tool contract a reference resolves to; AID-H-018.002 decides whether the authenticated principal may invoke it for the requested object and action.
Resolution establishes identity, not runtime authorization.

families.name: Unsafe Code Execution Prevention
families.description_text: Prevent unexpected code execution (RCE) through unsafe evaluation paths by banning dangerous constructs, enforcing safe interpreters, and requiring a pre-execution static scan gate for agent-generated code. This is a cheap, fail-fast preventive layer that complements sandbox containment and dynamic behavioral analysis.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Groups preventive controls that reject dangerous executable content before use or constrain it to an approved restricted interpreter. It does not provide the operating-system, container, or WASM containment boundary for arbitrary execution.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-025 prevents or narrows unsafe evaluation paths before execution; AID-I-001 contains code that is permitted to execute.
Static or interpreter-level restrictions cannot replace an independently enforced sandbox.

families.name: Continuous Closed-Loop Hardening of Retrainable Prompt Injection Detectors
families.description_text: Continuously strengthen a retrainable prompt injection detection model through a governed, closed-loop hardening pipeline. The pipeline generates or collects adversarial prompts that evade the current detector, identifies hard samples from detector errors, reinjects those samples into subsequent training cycles, and validates candidate detector versions on an independent out-of-loop evaluation set before promotion.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns the governed hard-sample, adversarial-corpus, coverage-analysis, retraining, and independent-promotion loop for a prompt-injection detector whose training lifecycle the organization controls. It does not perform inline runtime filtering.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-026 improves a retrainable detector between releases; AID-D-001.001 analyzes each live prompt and emits the runtime finding.
Offline detector hardening does not admit or block a production request.

AID-H-026 owns the closed-loop retraining lifecycle for prompt-injection detectors; AID-H-036 owns multilingual and locale-stratified validation evidence for inbound safety classifiers before promotion.
A retraining loop can consume multilingual results, but it does not replace language-segment evaluation.

families.name: MCP & Tool Client Security Hardening
families.description_text:
Harden the MCP or tool client itself - the local runtime, SDK, IDE extension, CLI client, or desktop application that sends requests to remote MCP servers, stores credentials, caches server responses, and mediates user permissions. The supported baseline is MCP v2 2026-07-28: initialize/notifications/initialized and Mcp-Session-Id are absent, protocol version and client capabilities travel in required per-request metadata, optional clientInfo carries self-reported client name and version when supplied, and explicit application handles carry cross-call state.

Coverage includes:

- Validating remote server authenticity before discovery or request dispatch.
- Protecting locally stored credentials and tokens from extraction.
- Preventing sensitive data from leaking through client-managed logs, caches, temporary files, or crash artifacts.
- Preventing malicious server responses from triggering client-side code execution or unsafe rendering.
- Isolating per-server request context, cache scope, credentials, and explicit application state.
- Verifying client binary, plugin, and update integrity.

Release gate: pin the 2026-07-28 specification, authoritative v2 schema, official SDK v2 artifacts, and conformance fixtures. Reject any request whose declared version differs. Negative fixtures must prove handshake methods and session headers cannot create protocol state.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns MCP and tool client or host security: remote-server trust, local credential storage, client-controlled data artifacts, response rendering, request and cache isolation, client distribution integrity, user-facing multi-round-trip input, and deprecated client sampling exceptions.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-028 owns the client and host side of MCP interactions; AID-H-034 owns server transport, publication, handler authorization, output, explicit-state, task, subscription, budget, and disable enforcement.
A control must be implemented at the side that owns the vulnerable state or decision.

AID-H-028 hardens the selected client's connection and local behavior; AID-H-024 resolves the intended logical server, tool, version, and descriptor contract.
Client hardening does not correct ambiguous or poisoned resolution.

AID-H-028 owns MCP client and host security, including credentials, rendering, local state, and client distribution; AID-H-004.005 supplies conditional end-to-end message integrity and replay protection when the client's communication path crosses untrusted or asynchronous intermediaries.
Client hardening alone does not preserve one message across a multi-hop path.

families.name: AI Data-Use Authorization & Lifecycle-Stage Boundary Enforcement
families.description_text:
Enforce purpose-bound, lifecycle-stage-aware authorization controls on data consumed by or generated within AI systems.

Operationalization: The technique operationalizes consent scope, contractual purpose limitations, jurisdictional restrictions, and internal data classification policies into machine-enforceable gates at each lifecycle-stage boundary.

Examples:

- Customer service transcripts authorized for real-time support but prohibited from fine-tuning.
- Legal documents authorized for RAG retrieval but prohibited from long-term memory.
- HR data authorized for summarization but prohibited from shared indexes or retraining corpora.

Google SAIF risk categories EDH (Excessive Data Handling) and UTD (Unauthorized Training Data) map directly to this technique's scope.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns machine-enforced decisions about whether a data asset may be used for a declared AI purpose and lifecycle stage, including training, evaluation, indexing, inference, logging, memory, and retraining. It does not establish provenance, authorize runtime sinks, or enforce retention duration.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-029 enforces permitted purpose and lifecycle-stage use; AID-M-002 records provenance, lineage, integrity, and risk evidence about the asset.
Knowing where data came from does not decide whether it may be used for a particular purpose.

AID-H-029 decides whether data may participate in a lifecycle stage or purpose; AID-H-018.005 constrains where specific values may flow at runtime and which sinks may receive them.
Authorized use does not authorize every destination, and an allowed sink does not authorize an otherwise prohibited purpose.

AID-H-029 controls whether data may enter or remain authorized for a stage; AID-I-004.005 enforces how long retained memory may persist and proves forgetting.
Use authorization and retention duration are independent policy dimensions.

families.name: Agentic Skill Admission Security Analysis & Control Pipeline
families.description_text:
Subject every agentic AI skill to a mandatory, multi-stage security analysis pipeline before it is approved for installation or execution in an enterprise environment.

Why skills need dedicated admission analysis: Skills are hybrid artifacts simultaneously containing executable code (shell scripts, Python calls), structured configuration (YAML frontmatter, JSON manifests, dependency files), natural-language behavioral instructions (Markdown prose directing agent actions), and self-declared metadata (name, author, permissions, risk tier) - no single scanning approach can adequately assess the security posture of such a composite artifact. The Snyk ToxicSkills research (February 2026) confirmed that malicious skills commonly combined both the code and natural language instruction layers as attack vectors, with pattern-matching scanners missing threats expressed entirely in prose.

Pipeline stages:

- AID-H-030.004 - Safe skill parsing & loader hardening
- AID-H-030.001 - Metadata honesty validation
- AID-H-030.002 - Instruction-layer semantic intent analysis
- AID-H-030.003 - Manifest-vs-observed behavioral consistency testing
- AID-H-030.005 - Admission policy orchestration & continuous re-scan governance

The pipeline renders block/review/allow decisions via a configurable policy engine. It operates at two deployment points: publish-time (for registry operators) and install-time (for enterprises using private skill mirrors or CI/CD).

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns the skill-specific admission pipeline that parses composite skill artifacts, evaluates metadata honesty and instruction intent, compares declared and observed behavior, and fuses exact stage evidence into a block, review, or allow decision. It orchestrates but does not reimplement generic scanners, publisher controls, capability enforcement, or sandboxes.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-030 admits third-party or externally sourced agentic skill packages; AID-H-031 governs internally AI-generated or AI-materially-modified development changes through the organization's SDLC.
Both use staged evidence, but their artifact trust models and promotion destinations differ.

AID-H-030 decides whether a skill artifact may be installed based on its declared and observed behavior; AID-H-018.007 defines and enforces the approved capability manifest at runtime.
Admission of a skill does not grant its requested capabilities.

AID-H-030 supplies skill-specific scenarios, manifest comparison, and the final admission policy; AID-I-001.005 owns generic isolated behavioral execution, observation completeness, teardown proof, and the attested report.
A clean sandbox report is one admission input rather than installation authorization.

families.name: AI-Generated Code Admission Control & Safe Promotion
families.description_text:
Establish a dedicated admission-and-promotion control plane for AI-generated or AI-materially-modified development artifacts before they are merged, built, released, or deployed. This family technique treats generated source code, infrastructure-as-code, workflow definitions, dependency changes, deployment manifests, installer or build scripts, repository automation code, and agent-authored patches as high-risk artifacts that require provenance labeling, policy evaluation, exploitability-oriented validation, and evidence-bound promotion decisions.

Why this exists: classic secure SDLC controls usually assume that a human authored the change and that reviewers can reason about intent line-by-line. AI-assisted development breaks that assumption: defenders need machine-enforced gates that can keep pace with rapid generation while still requiring higher-friction review for privileged or destructive paths.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns provenance-aware, risk-tiered admission and promotion of AI-generated or AI-materially-modified source code, infrastructure-as-code, workflows, dependency changes, deployment definitions, build scripts, and repository automation through the organization's SDLC.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-031 governs internally generated development changes through merge, build, release, and deployment; AID-H-030 admits externally sourced agentic skill artifacts for installation or execution.
The artifact origin, review context, and authorized destination determine which family owns the decision.

AID-H-031 governs the additional provenance and promotion risk created by AI-authored development changes; AID-H-003 governs general AI or ML supply-chain component integrity and admission.
AI-generated changes still pass ordinary supply-chain controls.

families.name: Multi-Tenant Inference Isolation & Leakage Prevention
families.description_text:
Reduce cross-tenant leakage risk in shared AI inference infrastructure and third-party AI SaaS by enforcing tenancy-aware isolation for compute, serving state, cache layers, telemetry, and tenant-verifiable provider isolation evidence. This family technique addresses the reality that shared LLM or model-serving environments can expose prompts, context, outputs, model internals, or request patterns through state reuse, side channels, insufficient cache isolation, profiling surfaces, or weak provider isolation evidence.

Why this exists: accelerator hygiene and confidential computing are necessary but not sufficient. Enterprises increasingly consume inference as a service; they therefore need controls that govern which workloads may run on shared serving pools, what tenancy guarantees the provider must prove, and how serving-state leakage is prevented at runtime.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns confidentiality isolation for shared or external inference services across capacity, serving state, tenant placement, profiling and debug surfaces, and provider evidence. It addresses service-tenancy leakage rather than generic output policy or component integrity.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-032 owns shared-serving and tenant-placement isolation; AID-H-009.004 owns accelerator residue clearing and low-level compute hygiene.
Clean VRAM does not isolate queues or KV caches, and logical tenant isolation does not prove hardware residue removal.

AID-H-032 governs the broader shared inference topology and tenant boundary; AID-H-027 governs authenticity, context binding, and safe reuse of individual cache objects.
Serving isolation must consume correct cache decisions without collapsing into cache implementation.

families.name: AI Gateway Routing Integrity & Policy-Preserving Failover
families.description_text:
Treat the AI gateway or model router as a security control plane, not merely a latency or cost optimization layer. This technique governs how requests are bound to approved models, providers, regions, remote MCP/A2A endpoints, and fallback paths so that routing changes do not silently weaken safety, compliance, data residency, retention, or approval constraints.

Coverage includes:

- Binding each request to an approved requested-vs-effective model record.
- Preventing silent failover to unapproved or less-safe models.
- Constraining routing by region, data zone, residency, and retention policy.
- Versioning, approving, canarying, and rolling back route policy bundles as security artifacts.
- Resolving and enforcing the final provider route immediately before dispatch.
- Resolving and enforcing effective sampling, output, log-probability, and provider safety-profile settings immediately before provider serialization.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns the AI gateway or model router decision plane that resolves and enforces the effective model, provider, account, endpoint, region, approved fallback, route policy, and invocation configuration. It does not resolve tools or authorize their effects.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-033 resolves model-provider routes and invocation settings; AID-H-024 resolves tool and MCP identities, versions, descriptors, and contracts.
Both are resolution controls, but over different namespaces and dispatch targets.

AID-H-033 decides which model endpoint is policy-eligible and should receive the request; AID-I-002.002 decides which external destinations are reachable at the network boundary.
An eligible route still requires network enforcement, and a reachable endpoint is not necessarily an approved route.

families.name: MCP Server Runtime Boundary & Tool Exposure Governance
families.description_text:
Harden the MCP server as an independent trust boundary that publishes tools, resources, prompts, multi-round-trip input requests, extension tasks, MCP Apps, and backend integrations. The supported baseline is MCP v2 2026-07-28: each Streamable HTTP request is self-contained, the initialize lifecycle and session ID are absent, routing headers match the JSON-RPC body, required per-request metadata carries protocol version and client capabilities, optional clientInfo carries self-reported client name and version when supplied, and application state uses explicit authorized handles.

Coverage includes:

- Deployment profile, stdio and Streamable HTTP transport, Origin, protocol/header validation, TLS, runtime, and coarse abuse baseline.
- OAuth protected-resource behavior, issuer and audience validation, progressive scope minimization, no token passthrough, and confused-deputy prevention.
- Validation and authorization before handlers, reads, prompts, backend calls, filesystem access, command execution, database queries, or network fetches.
- Signed publication contracts, JSON Schema 2020-12, ttlMs/cacheScope, extension negotiation, and MCP App declarations.
- Output, resource URI, explicit handles, Tasks/subscriptions, authoritative operation-budget integration, protocol-specific replay safeguards, and signed disable-state enforcement.

Release gate: pin exact MCP v2 2026-07-28 sources and conformance fixtures. Reject any request whose declared version differs, and prove forbidden handshake methods or session headers cannot create state.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns MCP server protocol and handler enforcement: deployment and transport baseline, OAuth resource semantics, backend authorization, publication, output, explicit application handles, task and subscription isolation, operation-budget integration, and authoritative disable-state checks.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-034 owns the MCP server and its backend boundary; AID-H-028 owns the client host, local credentials, rendering, client cache and state, user input flow, and client distribution.
Each side must enforce the state and decisions it controls.

AID-H-034 enforces authorization after a request reaches the MCP server; AID-H-018 defines and enforces the agent or orchestrator's capability policy before and during action execution.
Server-side authorization remains mandatory even for an approved agent request.

AID-H-034 governs what the server publishes and executes; AID-H-024 verifies consuming-side resolution of server, tool, descriptor, and contract identity.
A correctly hardened server does not prevent a client from resolving the wrong server.

AID-H-034 emits protocol and enforcement events at server handlers; AID-D-005.001 owns security telemetry generation contracts, collection, completeness, and durable observability across the AI system.
The server must provide events but must not claim end-to-end telemetry coverage.

AID-H-034 owns MCP-specific transport, OAuth, request and handle authorization, Tasks, subscriptions, budget hooks, idempotency boundaries, and disable-state enforcement; AID-H-004.005 owns a generic signed-envelope freshness and replay discipline across untrusted intermediaries.
MCP-specific mechanisms remain in AID-H-034 and do not amount to universal end-to-end message protection.

families.name: Reasoning-State Security & Compute Controls
families.description_text: Protect extended-thinking state as sensitive internal data and bounded compute. Separate raw-trace confidentiality/storage, provider-block round-trip integrity, and reasoning-compute budgets. Structured state transitions may be audited under AID-H-017.001; raw chain-of-thought is not required.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Groups controls for confidentiality and storage of reasoning traces, provider reasoning-block continuity, and reasoning-specific compute budgets. It does not require collection of raw chain-of-thought or own general agent state-transition auditability.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-037 protects hidden reasoning data and compute; AID-H-017.001 makes structured agent control-loop state interruptible and auditable.
Auditable state transitions do not require disclosure or retention of raw chain-of-thought.

families.name: Inference Serving Runtime Surface & Privileged Capability Governance
families.description_text: Constrain the process-level network surface and privileged capabilities of self-hosted or operator-controlled inference runtimes. Verify which listeners and internal transports actually start, and separately authorize state-changing runtime operations such as model load, unload, weight or adapter update, pause, resume, scaling, and repository control.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns inference-runtime listener and protocol conformance plus operation-level authorization of privileged or state-changing serving capabilities. It does not own TLS, caller authentication, network reachability policy, debug-output content, generic service discovery, vulnerability remediation, or model-interface composition.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-H-038.001 verifies which listeners and protocols the inference process actually starts; AID-I-002 controls which network sources can reach an approved endpoint.
A blocked unexpected port is still an unnecessary process surface, while an approved listener still requires network containment.

AID-H-004.002 establishes and authenticates the calling workload or service; AID-H-038.002 decides which authenticated identity may invoke each privileged inference-runtime operation.
Authentication without operation authorization does not protect weight update, adapter load, pause, scale, or model-control functions.

AID-H-038.001 determines whether a debug or metrics listener should exist and where it binds; AID-H-032.003 governs whether debug and observability output discloses sensitive information.
A listener can conform while leaking data, or expose no sensitive content while still being an unnecessary attack surface.

families.name: Adversarial Input, Prompt Injection & Signal-Authenticity Detection
families.description_text: Detect adversarial or policy-relevant properties intrinsic to an input, recalled memory item, or prompt-gate event: malicious intent and obfuscation, statistically anomalous vectors, prompt-integrity canary failures, forensic evidence that an image, voice, video, biometric, or other sensor signal is synthetic or manipulated, recalled-memory hazards, and decision-telemetry inconsistencies. Each child emits structured findings and evidence without making the admission or containment decision.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns findings about adversarial or policy-relevant properties intrinsic to an input, recalled memory item, media signal, or prompt-gate event. It detects and correlates evidence but does not admit, sanitize, block, downgrade, or contain the input.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-D-001 detects malicious content, anomalous vectors, prompt-integrity failures, or authenticity properties within an input or signal; AID-D-007 detects semantic, temporal, or payload inconsistency between modalities or across a multimodal session.
A suspicious property inside one artifact and a contradiction between multiple artifacts are different detector populations.

families.name: AI Model Anomaly & Performance Drift Detection
families.description_text:
Monitor deployed AI systems for statistically significant shifts in input distributions, output behavior, labeled performance, and available model telemetry. Where an operator can lawfully observe an emitted reasoning trace, inspect its meaning for attack or policy-evasion signals without treating it as a faithful record of internal cognition. This family groups detective controls for drift, poisoning effects, evasion symptoms, backdoor activation, reasoning abuse, and reasoning-specific resource anomalies.

Applicability: select only the sub-technique whose required signal is actually observable. An absent label stream, log-probability distribution, internal tensor, reasoning metadata, or emitted reasoning trace provides no evidence that the corresponding anomaly is absent.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns production detection of statistically significant shifts in input distributions, output behavior, labeled performance, model-internal signals, reasoning metadata, and the semantics of an operator-visible emitted reasoning trace. Each claim is limited to the exact observable signal and measured population.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-D-002 compares live behavior against approved references and emits drift or anomaly findings; AID-M-003.002 creates and recalibrates the trusted general predictive and operational baselines.
Production monitoring consumes a versioned reference rather than training on the same live population it judges.

families.name: AI Output Monitoring & Policy-Violation Detection
families.description_text: Inspect model outputs, classifications, streaming responses, agent tool proposals, and related session telemetry in near real time. Emit structured findings for safety, privacy, security, integrity, and business-policy violations.
