scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns near-real-time observation, classification, scoring, correlation, and alert evidence for policy-relevant model outputs, streaming responses, agent action proposals, and session effects. It does not enforce schemas, sanitize, block, render, authorize, release, or contain output.

families.name: AI Artifact, Runtime Configuration, Route & Lifecycle Integrity Monitoring
families.description_text: Detect unauthorized or unexplained changes to AI model and data artifacts, confidential-runtime attestations, runtime-loaded code and modules, runtime configuration and policy, requested-versus-effective routes, and observed lifecycle transitions.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns integrity and drift findings across static artifacts, confidential-runtime attestations, loaded code, runtime configuration, model sources, turn chains, effective routes, and lifecycle paths. Each child retains a separate measured population, prerequisite, and observation point.

families.name: AI Activity Logging, Monitoring & Threat Hunting
families.description_text: Establish auditable AI security telemetry and use it for monitoring, alerting, investigation, and hypothesis-driven threat hunting. Cover the relevant request, response, identity, model, agent, tool, data-access, cost, infrastructure, and error events without treating hidden reasoning or raw sensitive content as ordinary log data.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns the logging, rule-delivery, monitoring, investigation, hunting, triage, sensor-health, and volatile-evidence functions built on AI security telemetry. Logging an event does not by itself prove that a specialized detector identified the associated threat.

families.name: Multimodal Inconsistency Detection
families.description_text: For AI systems processing multiple input modalities such as text, image, document, audio, video, camera feeds, or screen shares, detect inconsistencies, contradictions, hidden cross-modal instruction patterns, and modality-specific anomaly signals before they are trusted as unified request or response context.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns findings for semantic, temporal, or payload inconsistency across multiple modalities, batch artifacts, and realtime sessions. It is partitioned by processing mode rather than by privileged modality and does not sanitize, admit, block, or gate the input.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-D-007 detects inconsistency between modalities or over a live multimodal session; AID-D-001 detects adversarial content, anomaly, canary, memory, or authenticity properties within an individual input or signal.
Cross-modal contradiction and artifact-local threat evidence require separate findings even when they occur together.

families.name: Fact Assurance & Multi-Agent Hallucination Detection
families.description_text: Detect unsupported, contradicted, stale, or weakly grounded factual claims and identify their propagation across agent boundaries.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns evidence-derived factual claim state and cross-agent propagation findings. It does not write to memory, approve an action, enforce a block, authenticate the transport, or treat peer agreement as truth.

families.name: Registered Agent Behavior, Interaction & Identity-Abuse Detection
families.description_text: Continuously detect whether a registered agent or AI non-human identity is behaving abnormally, whether authenticated inter-agent interaction events violate their contract, whether the registered population has drifted, or whether valid workload, service-principal, OAuth, connector, or delegated credentials are being abused. The children separately own behavior analytics, interaction-event contract monitoring, registered-population drift, and identity or token abuse.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns behavior, interaction-contract, registered-population, and identity or token-abuse findings for known agents and registered non-human identities. Unknown identities and reputation-based escalation belong to AID-D-016; authorization and response remain separate controls.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-D-011 evaluates known registered agents and identities against approved behavior, interaction, population, and token expectations; AID-D-016 discovers unknown or emergent agents and produces reputation-based escalation signals.
Registered-subject analytics and unknown-subject discovery start from different identity populations.

families.name: GNN Trigger-Response & Graph Anomaly Detection
families.description_text: Group three non-overlapping GNN detection mechanisms: candidate-model trigger response, structure-feature edge anomalies, and topology-only node anomalies. Each child defines its technical asset prerequisites and exact measured population; a genuinely non-graph asset or an absent feature/topology capability is distinct from missing artifacts or incomplete coverage.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns three distinct graph and GNN detector classes: validation-time candidate trigger response, structure-feature edge anomalies, and topology-only node anomalies. It consumes signed graph references but does not create baselines, mutate graphs, harden training, or treat missing applicable evidence as clean.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-D-012 executes graph and GNN detection against approved references; AID-M-003.006 creates, validates, signs, and recalibrates graph snapshots, metrics, and probe-output baselines.
Detection findings must remain independent of baseline authorship.

families.name: RAG Content, Relevance & Retrieval-Provenance Monitoring
families.description_text:
Monitor a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system at the post-retrieval, pre-context-assembly observation point across three distinct axes:

- Content: detect malicious instructions, payloads, or policy violations inside retrieved chunks.
- Relevance: detect query-to-chunk semantic mismatch and abnormal retrieval scores against a calibrated reference.
- Retrieval provenance and coverage: check the ordered top-k population, source identity and registry membership, expected-versus-returned count, diversity, and source-concentration policy.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns post-retrieval, pre-context-assembly findings across malicious chunk content, query-to-document relevance, and ordered retrieval provenance, diversity, and coverage. It does not mutate the index, remove chunks, decide final admission, or perform request-ingress detection.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-D-014 analyzes chunks and retrieval populations after the RAG lookup; AID-D-001 analyzes user inputs, recalled memory, media authenticity, and prompt-gate signals at ingress or rehydration.
The same malicious pattern can require separate findings because the source, identity, and observation point differ.

AID-D-014 emits RAG content, relevance, provenance, diversity, and coverage findings; AID-H-020 enforces retrieval integrity, authorization, signing, and hygiene.
Detection reports suspicious retrieval, while Harden controls which chunks may enter context.

families.name: Rogue Agent Discovery & Reputation Escalation
families.description_text: Detect previously unseen or newly emergent agent identities and communication edges, then combine signals from separate security detectors into auditable reputation and escalation findings. This Detect family does not quarantine, evict, or restore agents.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns discovery of previously unseen or newly emergent agent identities and communication edges, followed by auditable reputation and escalation findings. It does not quarantine, evict, or restore agents.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-D-016 discovers and scores unknown or emergent agents; AID-D-011 evaluates behavior, interaction evidence, population drift, and token abuse for registered identities.
Unknown-subject discovery and known-subject analytics must not share an assumed approved baseline.

families.name: AI Execution Sandboxing & Runtime Isolation
families.description_text: Execute AI models, autonomous agents, or individual AI tools and plugins within isolated environments such as sandboxes, containers, or microVMs. These environments must be configured with strict limits on resources, permissions, and network connectivity. The primary goal is that if an AI component is compromised or behaves maliciously, the impact is confined to the isolated sandbox, preventing harm to the host system or lateral movement.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns isolation of AI models, agents, and tools inside bounded execution environments with constrained resources, permissions, filesystems, and network access. It confines a compromised runtime; it does not sanitize web content, isolate browser-managed task state, or confine an embedded client-side model inside the user's application runtime.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-I-001 isolates server-side or managed AI execution environments; AID-I-007 confines a client-side model or model runtime inside a browser, Electron shell, hybrid app, or mobile application.
Use AID-I-007 for component-level Web Worker, iframe, WASM, CSP, and native-bridge boundaries inside the client application, not as a substitute for the enclosing managed sandbox family.

AID-I-001 isolates execution processes and tool runtimes; AID-I-008 isolates browser-managed and desktop-workspace state per task or trust zone.
A process sandbox does not by itself rotate cookies, browser storage, downloads, clipboard, history, desktop profiles, or authenticated computer-use state.

AID-I-001 contains a process, container, microVM, WASM, or other workload boundary; AID-H-018.009 confines the particular filesystem object that a model-influenced path may open or affect, including in-process tools.
Isolation and opened-object confinement remain independently applicable and neither PASS substitutes for the other.

AID-I-001 contains execution after an AI development client starts a task, tool, extension, server, or other workload; AID-H-021.005 decides whether the exact repository-controlled activation manifest may leave restricted mode in the first place.
A sandbox does not approve workspace activation, and a trusted activation manifest does not prove runtime containment.

families.name: Network Segmentation & Isolation for AI Systems
families.description_text: Implement network segmentation and microsegmentation strategies using firewalls, proxies, private endpoints, and transport layer security to enforce strict communication boundaries for AI systems. This involves isolating internal components (e.g., training vs. inference environments, data stores) to limit lateral movement, and securing connections to external dependencies (e.g., MaaS APIs) to prevent data exfiltration, SSRF, and MitM attacks. The goal is to reduce the blast radius of a compromise by enforcing least-privilege network access both internally and externally.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns network segmentation, microsegmentation, private connectivity, egress mediation, and measured reachability for internal and external AI communication paths, including agent listeners, discovery endpoints, callbacks, brokers, relays, and direct peer routes. It limits which identities and routes can connect but does not establish message identity or authorize message content.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-I-002 controls network reachability between AI and agent components; AID-H-004.003 authenticates peer identity, protects channel and message integrity, prevents replay, and authorizes the A2A task.
A permitted network path is not proof that a peer message is authentic or authorized, and secure messaging does not replace network segmentation.

families.name: Quarantine & Throttling of AI Interactions
families.description_text:
Contain suspicious AI activity by degrading, rate-limiting, quarantining, or blocking the specific identity, session, tenant, agent instance, resource budget, or high-risk action that is creating risk.

Control families: child controls separate detection-driven quarantine and safe mode, identity/session/API throttling, resource-token-spend budget throttling, and per-action containment before side effects. This split reflects real engineering ownership: SecOps/SOAR, API gateway, platform/FinOps, and agent orchestration teams.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns reversible response-time containment after a detection, policy, health, trust-state, or budget signal crosses a containment threshold. It translates existing findings into bounded quarantine, degradation, rate limiting, budget throttling, or per-action enforcement; it does not compute the signal or perform durable eviction.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-I-003 applies reversible quarantine, safe mode, throttling, or action containment; AID-E-002 revokes execution leases and terminates confirmed-compromised runtime processes, jobs, pods, and containers.
Use this family for bounded containment while investigation or recovery proceeds, and E-002 when the incident decision requires authoritative live-execution eviction.

AID-I-003 contains a scoped identity, session, tenant, agent, budget, or action; AID-I-005 applies a last-resort system-wide or tenant-wide halt or severe restriction.
A local quarantine or throttle is not proof that the emergency halt propagated across every required execution boundary.

AID-I-003 applies reversible quarantine, safe-mode downgrade, or throttling while investigation and recovery proceed; AID-E-001 authoritatively revokes compromised credentials, sessions, principals, issuance paths, and delegated grants after an incident decision.
A quarantine receipt cannot prove durable identity-plane eviction, and revocation does not replace bounded containment of the affected workload or action.

families.name: Agent Memory & State Isolation
families.description_text:
Protect agent context, tool traces, peer-agent messages, and persistent memory from prompt-injection persistence, poisoning, unauthorized mutation, secret carryover, and cross-session or cross-tenant contamination.

The sub-techniques separately govern runtime context boundaries, persistent-store partitioning, cryptographic read/write integrity, quarantine-to-trusted memory promotion, retention, protected identity files, task-phase demotion, summary/compaction integrity, and peer-message quarantine before active-context admission. Select only the children that match the system's actual memory and state architecture.

families.name: Task-Scoped Browser & Computer-Use Workspace Isolation for Agents
families.description_text:
Isolate browser and desktop computer-use agents per task or trust zone across browser context, profile, origin, workspace, and OS-automation boundaries. Cover cookies, local storage, IndexedDB, cache, history, downloads, clipboard, screenshots, desktop-session state, and automation permissions so hostile web content or residual authenticated state cannot cross task boundaries.

The children separately own ephemeral context lifecycle, cross-origin read/write segmentation, download and clipboard transfer quarantine, authentication-bearing navigation isolation, and disposable desktop workspaces with action confirmation.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns task- or trust-zone isolation of browser-managed state and disposable desktop computer-use workspaces, including contexts, profiles, origins, cookies, local storage, IndexedDB, cache, history, downloads, clipboard, screenshots, desktop-session state, and automation permissions.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-I-008 isolates browser-managed and desktop-workspace state around an agent task; AID-I-007 confines the client-side model or model-runtime component itself.
A sandboxed model component does not rotate authenticated browser state, and a fresh browser context does not prove that the embedded model runtime has a minimal capability boundary.

AID-I-008 isolates browser and desktop state after content is admitted to a computer-use workflow; AID-H-019 owns URL admission, safe fetch, content demotion, observation export, and the outer browser process boundary.
Safe content handling does not replace per-task state isolation, and an isolated workspace does not make an untrusted URL or observation safe.

AID-I-008 owns browser-context and desktop-workspace state lifecycle; AID-I-001.003 owns the enclosing single-use sandbox lifecycle and teardown.
A fresh browser profile can run inside a reused process sandbox, and a fresh process sandbox can still inherit browser-managed state unless both controls are enforced.

AID-I-008 isolates browser and desktop automation state; AID-I-004 isolates conversational context, tool traces, peer messages, and persistent agent memory.
Browser storage or clipboard cleanup does not prove model-context hygiene, and clearing agent memory does not remove cookies, downloads, desktop files, or authenticated browser residue.

families.name: Compromised Credential, Session, Principal & Grant Eviction
families.description_text: Evict compromised authentication and authorization objects from effective use after a verified incident by applying authoritative revocation to four non-overlapping populations: root or long-lived credential objects; already-issued tokens, authentication sessions, and leases; AI-agent or workload principals and their ability to obtain new credentials; and delegated grants or connected-app authorizations. Each child owns one object population and authoritative control plane, and evidence for one population does not prove eviction of another.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns authoritative incident-time eviction of four authentication and authorization object populations: root or long-lived credential objects, already-issued tokens and authentication sessions, AI-agent or workload principals and issuance paths, and delegated grants or connected-app authorizations. Evidence for one population does not prove eviction of another.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-001 revokes authentication and authorization objects; AID-E-002 terminates active processes, agent runs, execution leases, supervisor jobs, pods, and containers.
Credential or session revocation does not prove that compromised code stopped executing, and process termination does not revoke the identities or artifacts that could start new execution.

AID-E-001 evicts identity-plane credentials, sessions, principals, and grants; AID-E-005 removes durable application and agent state.
Application session records, conversational memory, webhook or tool registrations, queues, and schedules require separate teardown even after authentication objects are revoked.

AID-E-001 invalidates compromised or prior authentication and authorization state; AID-R-003.001 creates a new trusted interactive session after eviction.
Successful reauthentication does not prove that the old credential, token, grant, or session population was revoked, and eviction does not itself establish a recovered session.

AID-E-001 authoritatively and durably revokes compromised credentials, sessions, principals, issuance paths, and delegated grants; AID-I-003 applies reversible quarantine, safe-mode downgrade, throttling, or action containment while investigation or recovery proceeds.
Containment does not prove identity-plane eviction, and revocation does not replace immediate bounded control of the affected workload, session, or action.

families.name: Malicious AI Artifact Quarantine, Eviction & Recovery Routing
families.description_text: After an incident decision binds confirmed or policy-mandated malicious artifacts to exact immutable identities, quarantine or evict those artifacts and route non-detachable model impact to the canonical recovery owner. Apply only manifest-authorized removal or isolation, create durable tombstones, and make the complete affected artifact population ineligible for serving.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns manifest-authorized quarantine or eviction of confirmed malicious model, dataset, graph, adapter, code, and configuration artifacts; durable tombstone propagation; serving ineligibility; and routing of non-detachable model impact to recovery. Candidate discovery and compromise attribution remain inputs from Detect or validation controls.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-E-003 removes or quarantines malicious artifacts; AID-E-002 terminates active execution processes, leases, jobs, pods, and containers.
Artifact eviction prevents future serving or loading but does not prove that already running code stopped, while process termination leaves the malicious source artifact available unless this control removes it.

AID-E-003 makes the compromised model or adapter population ineligible and routes recovery; AID-R-001 restores or creates a trusted recovered model release.
Eviction does not establish recovered-model readiness, and successful model recovery does not prove removal of every compromised artifact or derivative.

families.name: Secure AI Model Restoration & Retraining
families.description_text: Restore an incident-affected model to a known-good state by either deploying an exact trusted pre-incident version or building a new remediated artifact through clean retraining when rollback is unavailable or untrustworthy.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns recovered-model readiness and release through either exact rollback or construction of a newly remediated model. It does not quarantine a suspect model, evict compromised adapters or derivatives, or remove malicious artifacts before recovery.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-001 restores and releases a trusted model state; AID-E-003 removes or quarantines malicious AI artifacts before recovery.
Recovery may consume AID-E-003 eviction evidence, but a successful rollback or retraining result does not prove that the compromised artifact was removed from every serving, registry, cache, or lineage path.

families.name: Trusted Identity, Context & Capability Re-establishment
families.description_text: After checking applicable eviction prerequisites against their signatures, digests, and authoritative readbacks, re-establish trusted interactive identities, clean conversational or agent context, and bounded runtime capabilities. These are separate recovery functions with different authoritative populations and enforcement points.

scope_boundary.responsibility: Owns creation of new post-incident identity sessions, restoration of selected clean conversational or agent state, and progressive re-enablement of capabilities. It consumes authoritative eviction results and does not duplicate revocation, durable-state teardown, transport hardening, user communications, or heightened monitoring.

related_techniques.comparison:
AID-R-003 creates new trusted identity and capability state after incident prerequisites pass; AID-E-001 revokes compromised credentials, sessions, principals, and grants.
A new recovery session or restored privilege cannot substitute for authoritative eviction of the prior authentication and authorization objects.

AID-R-003 restores selected clean application or agent state; AID-E-005 removes compromised durable sessions, memory, registrations, queues, and schedules.
Restoration must consume teardown evidence when applicable and must not reintroduce the state that AID-E-005 removed.
